Name: Tony Twillie
Question: When is the earliest you would draft a kicker in the NFL draft?
Answer: Depends. What is my team like? Do I have few other spaces that I need filled? For the teams that drafted kickers early, that’s not me. I could never use a first round pick on a person who could potentially not appear or factor in a game. How do I justify spending big on a guy who might not appear at all, or maybe just once a game? I used a first round pick on that? Plus, the financials of it make it crazy - draft a kicker first round and they’re going to get a minimum of about $4 million a year. Justin Tucker is the best kicker in the league and he only makes $6 million a year. I think personally the earliest I could take a kicker would maybe be late 3rd round. I’d feel better with a 4th round pick on a kicker. There is makes more financial sense and I got my guy if I really felt that strongly about them.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Given that Mac Jones has the NFL highest passer rating during the 2024 preseason, should the Patriots have kept Mac Jones rather than trade him for a 6th round pick which arguably does not compensate for the dead cap space incurred by the trade?
Answer: Second part first - we have no idea what the value of that trade is until we see what Joe Milton III does. That’s the pick the Patriots got from Jax. If Milton wins the QB job in New England at some point, then we can begin to assess the value of that trade. Financially speaking, the dead money was only $2.1 million, so not a big hit. Highest passer rating in preseason is like saying the Lions went undefeated in preseason in 2008. No disrespect to Jones, but he’s throwing well against guys who aren’t likely to be starters for their teams. Maybe he’s better than with the Patriots. We all know they had a terrible OC situation during Jones’ time there. But they were drafting a QB regardless, so Jones was still looking at being a backup. And once they’d decided to bring back Jacoby Brissett, that was pretty much the end of days for Jones. Even if Jones went off and became an NFL stud, I don’t think the Patriots will regret letting him go. Bad marriage. They felt they needed to start fresh and he needed a fresh start too.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do you think the Giants should have drafted a quarterback instead of Malik Nabers in the 2024 NFL Draft?
Answer: You - unwisely - re-upped Daniel Jones at a high dollar amount. Can’t trade him because he has no trade value and never did. He kills you in dead cap if you release him. And if you draft another guy and bench Jones, you feel like morons paying your backup starter money. Giants made errors, and they have to live with them, at least through this season. After 2024, you can get out for $22.2 million in dead cap. Still a big chunk of change, but not unmanageable when the cap keeps increasing 10–12% every year. Bringing a QB in this year would have created a controversy and you’re trying to win football games in New York. The media is already big and on your butt, you don’t need an extra ring for that circus. Nabers is a safe pick. Barring injury, he’s going to be a solid receiver for you for the foreseeable future, and regardless of the QB. Unless Jones steps up and has an injury free season and throws for 4000+ yards and 30+ TDs, next offseason you’ll target a QB.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: A recent anonymous poll of NFL players stated that Josh Allen, QB of the Buffalo Bills, is the most overrated quarterback in the NFL, followed by Jalen Hurts and Tua Tagovailoa. What's the basis for their peers rating these players as overrated?
Answer: Hard to say what motivates players to place negative ratings on their peers. Some of it is that they are human and really don’t know what it means to rate players. I’m sure some is based on personal experience. Some is based on preferences. And some is based on the same things that fans base it on - numbers/wins and losses. Allen “can’t” be as good as - say - Lamar because he doesn’t have 2 MVPs. Can’t be as good at Mahomes because he has no rings. So players get thrown by comparisons. But if we say Allen isn’t good because he’s not Lamar or Mahomes, that’s really unfair. Players can be good and not be the very best. Goff isn’t the best - that doesn’t mean he’s not good. In all honesty, the reason players say that is because people ask that. Back in the day, the respect was so deep no one would ask that question, and no one would answer it if asked Players talk now more than ever, and are more willing to speak their minds, even when it’s not the best thing to do.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why did the Raiders hire Tom Telesco as GM after he did such a poor job building the Chargers roster?
Answer: Just as there are only a few people truly qualified to be NFL head coaches, there are few people qualified to be NFL GMs. The Raiders had fired a GM and a coach. It’s never a great move to bring in a rookie coach AND a rookie GM. They needed at least one of them to be experienced. And since the GM was hired before the coach was announced, it was Telesco. The Chargers’ roster was always uneven - good offense but a less than good defense or vice versa. Telesco had 11 seasons to get things right. He hired 3 coaches. Nothing worked. From an outside standpoint, it seems very much like Telesco’s fault. But we also saw coaching that was obviously less than good. It may be that the Raiders felt like with the right coaching, Telesco could still put together a decent team. Remains to be seen.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Did the Raiders regret drafting JaMarcus Russell?
Answer: Of course they did, after the fact. But in the moment, you can only know what you know. And until he held out, then showed up out of shape at camp, you didn’t have any idea how bad it was going to be. You can ask a ton of questions, do all the research you want - you may still not get down to what makes a player tick, or how they might react to adversity. No one seemed to find out about Russell’s addiction to codeine and “purple drank” in the vetting process. You know what you know. You take the measurables and you hope you’re hitting on the person too. Obviously hindsight is 20/20 and of course in the aftermath there was regret. But you also have to say live and learn. It’s not as though Russell was a chump player and other teams weren’t also looking to draft him. He wasn’t getting past the first 3 slots in the draft, likely, with Detroit and Cleveland both needing QB help.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: When a football team drafts a player, but don’t sign him before a season starts, is he just out of a job, or what happens?
Answer: This rarely happens anymore, not since the NFL implemented the rookie salary scale. There is no more holding out for more money anymore, the only negotiations are signing bonus and what is guaranteed. In the event a player doesn’t sign, they are still the property of that team for a full year. The team might try to negotiate through the player’s agent to work out a trade situation. But the alternative would be that the team simply doesn’t have that player for the year. The following year, that player may re-enter the draft. If they still don’t sign with a team, they may become a free agent. Good luck signing with a team for anything more than peanuts when you’ve now sat out a year and have proven to be a malcontent. Usually things like this are known and worked out pre-draft. It was known that Eli Manning wasn’t going to play for the Chargers, so the Chargers worked out a trade before the draft even started with the Giants. They agreed to select each QB, then trade picks. That saved the Chargers from having to not be able to have their pick or a QB. It’s exceedingly rare for a player to simply not play. The most famous case was Bo Jackson. He was drafted by Tampa Bay, but because owner Hugh Culverhouse pulled some shenanigans that cost him the remainder of his baseball eligibility at Auburn, he refused to sign with them. He instead signed to play baseball with the Royals. The following season, the Raiders decided to take a flyer and drafted Bo in the 7th round of the draft the following year, and allowed him to play baseball and then come to football.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: In the NFL, is there a correlation between preseason record and regular season record?
Answer: I really don’t think much can be inferred by preseason records; moreso today than ever. In the past when teams played 4 preseason games, it was common for starters to play up to the first half of the 3rd preseason game, then maybe one series in the final game. There was a move to make sure you had enough on field game situation reps so that you’re not walking into week one never having thrown to your receivers, taken a handoff from your QB, or blocking alongside your teammates. Today, none of that exists. You may or may not see your starting QB take preseason game snaps. You may or may not see the starting RB play. It’s now frowned upon due to the risk of injury. In practice, even the ones against other teams, they have controlled scrimmages where QB’s cannot be hit and the tackling is less than aggressive. In preseason, those things don’t exist, so they often pull the starters. It’s why the NFL sucks and is so unpredictable in the first 2–3 weeks of the season, and why there are so many injuries early on. But I digress… Because we see so few starters, we can’t correlate any success or failure with the regular season. We see the starters a little and then a lot of the second teamers. So we can kind of know what might happen if a starter gets hurt, but we don’t see enough of what we’ll see in the regular season to make a difference. The only thing you can really take from watching preseason is the crispness of passes, the decision making of QBs, the burst from a RB, the route running and hands of the WR, does the offensive lineman consistently beat their man, does the defensive lineman consistently beat their man, can the LBs stay in position and tackle, and can the DB’s cover. That’s a lot, but remember, you’re basing that on just a small handful of plays by the first teamers on either side of the ball.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is Jerry Jones the reason Cowboys have not had any Post Season Success?
Answer: You have to say he’s at least part of the reason considering he’s the one constant of this entire stretch of almost 30 years without a ring. 13 playoff appearances, only 7 playoff games won over that stretch. Jones is not a team builder. He’s an acquirer of players, some very talented players. But never great teams. And you need to have winners top to bottom to have great opportunities to win. Jerry just doesn’t get that. And he’s too busy trying to be the face of the franchise to be the GM of the franchise. My statement remains - if Jerry the owner had another GM as unsuccessful as Jerry the GM, he would have fired him LONG ago.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Should NFL teams prefer to trade down their 1st/2nd-round draft picks for picks in the 3rd+ rounds given that the latter receive only guaranteed signing bonuses but not guaranteed salaries and therefore consume less dead cap space if they are cut?
Answer: It’s not that simple. You don’t mind paying money if you’re going to get a solid return on investment. Beyond that, you simply can’t comprise a strong NFL team of nothing but 3rd and lower round draft picks. Even the Chiefs, who are the gold standard today, have a lineup that is at least equal first two rounds guys and later guys. If it was realistic to get the same talent in every round, then every team would wait for that pick. Unfortunately, that’s not how it happens… The best teams are the ones who a) get lucky later in the draft, and/or b) know how to find diamonds in the rough - guys who are on the ascent and got overlooked, or are gamers whose measurables don’t necessarily show up in the combine. If you consistently trade out of the first two rounds, you’ll have a team that is not ready to compete with teams that have first and second round talent that did work out very well. As for dead cap space, on the rookie scale, if a young player doesn’t work out, that dead cap hit isn’t huge. And it’s rarely an issue. Guys drafted in the first two rounds are typically going to last 4–5 years. Even if the drafting team wants to get rid of them, they can find someone to trade for them usually. Every team thinks they can rehabilitate an underperforming player. It’s why Trey Lance is in Dallas. And he’s in his 4th season. If Dallas releases him, which I don’t think they did, they’d be on the hook for a $5.3 million cap hit. Big, but not insurmountable. But they’ll probably keep him for the season. He’s virtually untradable.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is Malik Willis an upgrade over Green Bay Packers backup quarterbacks Sean Clifford and Michael Pratt?
Answer: Pratt is a rookie, so Willis has experience over him. Clifford has been in the league a few seasons now, but hasn’t gotten any opportunity to get on the field. Clifford was a 5th round pick a season ago, and they drafted Pratt this year, so the writing was already on the wall for Clifford. When you draft QB’s in back to back seasons, it’s because you didn’t like what you had. Willis isn’t a great QB, but he’s still an interesting prospect to some scouts and front office guys. Maybe GB thinks their offense will suit him more and they can get more out of him? I don’t think he’s much an improvement over either of those guys (Clifford is allegedly the one to lose a spot). But if you have 2 QB’s with basically no NFL experience and you have the opportunity to bring in a guy who at least has some NFL starts under his belt, it’s got to be an upgrade.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How good would an NFL offense be if it had the best offensive line and middle-of-the-pack QB, running backs, and receivers?
Answer: Better than an offense with a middle of the pack offensive line, and the best QB, running backs, and receivers. Great offensive line play fixes a lot. Average QB’s become good QBs. Good QB’s become great. Running backs are now so much better since they have holes to run through. Receivers are better because their QB’s are protected well enough to deliver better passes. Contrast that with an average O-line. The QB now has just average protection and is constantly looking over their shoulder, making them less effective. RB’s don’t get holes to run through consistently, so they’re often looking to bounce outside, which isn’t always the best choice. WRs have to break more routes off short or have to adjust for poorer passes coming from QBs with less time to throw. Give me a great line every day - we’ll figure the rest of it out.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Will we ever see a new competitor league to the NBA one day? If so, how long?
Answer: Oh, I’m sure someday, some person will think they can start a competitor league and set out to do so. And they’ll end up like the World Basketball League or the International Basketball League. It won’t even be as fruitful as the ABA, where some teams were absorbed by the NBA. The cost is so prohibitive to start up a new league. Then the logistics - where do they play? When do they play? How to compete for the caliber of player worth spending money to see, like the NBA has? That’s really so much the issue - leagues come in thinking they can do a quality product on a shoestring budget. It’s much more expensive then you’d imagine.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why do you think golfers often get frustrated on the course?
Answer: Because golf is hard. It’s difficult to have a swing that repeats over and over again, yielding similar results. We’re just not that good. But when things do come together, you see what your game could be. And for many of us, it’s annoying as hell to know what you’re capable of but not accomplish it. You flush a nice drive, then flub your approach shot. You hit a great approach, but 3 putt. Very frustrating. You know you’re better than that, but you still fail to show it.

Answer: Which model was that? I saw a few and not one of them had Carr above those players. I do not subscribe to SportsLine so maybe it was something I’m not seeing.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do you think Mac Jones, who is the second successor to Tom Brady, and who directly followed after Cam Newton (Brady’s first successor in 2020), is much better off leaving to the Jaguars?
Answer: No, but it needed to happen. Jones was not going to be the starter in New England any longer. New coach, new regime. They were going to look for a new QB because despite the fact that Jones had little competence in the offensive coordinator department, he simply didn’t do well enough as an individual. They needed to start fresh in the post Belichick era. But remaining in New England would likely have left him as the backup to a rookie - a stronger position. And he’d be a known commodity to the staff that remained from Belichick, including the head coach. He should have wanted to stay there and take his chances unless he was going to get a starting job elsewhere. Football-wise, to go to be the backup behind a guy drafted to be the franchise guy, and paid like the franchise guy, is tough. This is the can’t miss guy who was drafted first in Jones’ draft class. Barring injury to Lawrence, the chance of Jones seeing much field time after pre-season is low. I’ll say he did make a decent decision for himself, though. He’s from Jacksonville, so he moved home. Even if football doesn’t work out well, he’s around friends and family.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Should the New Orleans Saints have signed Derek Carr as the replacement for longtime quarterback Drew Brees?
Answer: Well, if you recall, he wasn’t intended to be Brees’ replacement. Quick history - side note… Tom Brady had allegedly decided that he wanted to play in New Orleans with Sean Payton as his coach. He wanted to take over for Brees when he retired. And that looked to be happening, maybe as early as 2019 (after the 2018 season), had the Saints gone to the Super Bowl and faced Brady’s Patriots. But that didn’t happen as the Saints lost the NFC Championship. Brees signed a new deal and the Brady thing went away - until news noted that Sean Payton and Brady may have had a plan to meet in Miami. But that’s a separate story altogether. When Brees retired, Payton felt at least decent about the prospects of running with Jameis Winston. And Winston won the starting job, then began the season with a 5–2 record before having his ACL blown out. So the Saints never had any intent at that point to bring in Derek Carr, they were going with Winston. When Sean Payton left the Saints for “retirement”, it changed the dynamic. The Saints again went with Winston but Winston got hurt in the first game a struggled over the next 2 weeks before being replaced to allegedly rehab his injury. Andy Dalton was the backup and not intended to be Brees’ replacement. When Winston was healthy enough to play again, the team decided to continue with Dalton. It wasn’t until 2023 that they decided to bring in Carr, three seasons after Brees retired. So this wasn’t an effort to bring him in to replace Brees - it was simply trying to find their next QB. I think in reality, when you have one of the top 10–15 QBs in the history of the game, you’re not really ever going to “replace” him (unless you have the fortune and/or foresight of San Francisco or Green Bay).

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What does Trump mean by "Make America Great Again"? I agree America should be great, but what does he mean 'again'? What era does he want America to return to?
Answer: As an anti-MAGA person, I have little idea. But I think if you asked trump, he’d not necessarily be able to define the time. And the reality is the time frame isn’t completely the thing because during the time frame they’re probably referring to, tax on the wealthy was around 90%, and corporate taxes were in the 50% range. They’re not trying to do that again, even though that was part of what made America better financially. But what do they mean? White men were the dominant group; women, people of color, and homosexuals “knew their place” in society. No civil rights Mostly European immigrants Christianity as a religious backdrop They do mean better economy too, but - again - they have no idea why the economy was so much better in, say, the 1950’s, and it’s because the middle class didn’t bear the tax burden, hence everyone had more money.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is Patrick Mahomes the most entertaining quarterback to watch in the NFL?
Answer: If not, he’s certainly one of them. Some may appreciate Lamar Jackson confounding defenses more, but I my money would be on the sidearm throws, the underhand throws, the shovel passes, the throwing back across his body or back across the field, that we see from Mahomes. Lamar is like having the cheat codes or the joystick - Mahomes is like messing with the mother board…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Who is the golfer with the most major wins but has not won any PGA Tour events?
Answer: Well, the majors are co-opted by each major world tour, so if you win a major, you have by definition won a PGA Tour event. They count as wins on each of the two major tours - the US PGA Tour, and the DP Tour in Europe. So when you win the US Open, that win counts on the DP Tour as well. My guess is that everyone who has won more than one major has won at least a singular other tour event. There are a few guys like Shaun Micheel whose only PGA Tour win was his PGA Championship. He did win events on the Nike Tour and the Asian Tour as well. I’m sure there are a few others with one major win and no other wins. I couldn’t find anyone with more than one major who only won those majors and nothing else.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Are there any professional golfers who have achieved success on tour without having an ideal swing? If yes, who are they?
Answer: There are many guys who don’t have ideal swings and have had success. 2 off the top of my head… Allen Doyle’s swing looked like he was late for dinner. He parlayed that into 2 US Senior Open wins, among his 11 Champions Tour wins. He didn’t even play on the PGA Tour, opting to play mini-tours and operating a driving range until he was 46 years old. Jim Furyk is a 17 time winner on Tour, a major champion, and one of the few golfers in history to shoot a 59 or lower in a Tour event - and he did it twice, shooting a 58 and a 59. But that swing…. it’s ugly….

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why did the Kansas City Chiefs fire John Mackovic after he took the Chiefs to the playoffs for the first time in 15 years?
Answer: Sounds like because he was a tool. Players didn’t like him, he was losing a couple of coaches (one in a lateral move), and it just seemed that he wasn’t well liked. His demeanor was gruff and not appreciated. Bad “chemistry” is what the Hunts said was their reason for letting him go.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is Tua Tagovailoa worth the four-year, $212.4 million extension that the Dolphins gave him?
Answer: Based on history? Questionable. Great year last season, after an early career that saw him not able to stay on the field due to injury. He picked a great time to have his best year, and most healthy year, when it was crap or get off the pot with him. In the NFL, there’s Mahomes. Then there are guys who are great but haven’t can’t win the big ones - Allen, Jackson, Burrow (also with his own injury history…). Then there are guys good enough to get to the playoffs - Dak, Stafford, Rodgers. Tua is in a category just below this. Yeah, he’s been to the playoffs. But can he do it regularly? He’s in that Herbert category, but Herbert is a better thrower than Tua. I don’t know if that warrants $53 million a year. I think he was just the next guy up and that’s the way the money is handed out these days.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What do you think of Tua Tagovailoa's comments about Brian Flores?
Answer: TBH, I think Tua should have been more professional. We all get bored with coach speak and cliche player interviews - here is a place where a cliche interview would have been better. There’s no need to dunk on Flores. Bad relationship, fine. We already knew that; from draft day we knew that. It’s over, he’s gone, you’ve moved on. Be bigger. Grow. Speak in broad generalities. Or just say you’re not interested in talking about the past, you’re looking towards the future. It’s in poor taste. Not just that, but one day you’re going to face Flores, and you don’t want him to have ammunition against you.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Which NFL team do you believe has the most impressive wide receiver tandem for the 2024 season?
Answer: Because of their QB, the best IMO would be Jamarr Chase and Tee Higgins. There are a lot of other great ones but none of them have as talented a QB throwing to them. I know many will think first of Hill and Waddle, and I’ll admit my bias towards Burrow. But Tua is a liability at QB. He’s been injured too often. That said, I get it. Hill is a force by himself, so it’s hard to not take Hill and Waddle. And Hill’s greatness alone puts him in front of Chase. But I still have a lot of respect for Chase and Higgins. Give them 1 and 1a. Nacua and Cupp have to be up there too, but we’ll have to make sure Nacua is the real deal. Brown and Smith - gotta love the very common names - in Philly should get love, but Hurts and the Philly offense have to be better this year.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What is the most Fascinating Week 1 NFL Matchup?
Answer: I’ll give you four… Both season openers are great. You get a rematch of the AFC Championship with the Chiefs taking on the Ravens, and then on Friday you get the Packers and Eagles in Brazil. We get to find out if the Packers are really for real, and see if the Eagles’ collapse was exaggerated. Of course it’s week 1, so nothing will be etched in stone about the teams from their first games, but they are at least intriguing matchups. On Sunday, the Texans/Colts matchup is interesting. In a divisional matchup, will the Texans build on last season? And what does Anthony Richardson look like in year two after missing much of year one with a major injury? And the Sunday night game featuring the Rams and Lions should be fun. The two strong offensive teams, obviously the QB’s facing their old teams (though it’s been a few years and a few meetings already, so that novelty has worn off). The wild card I’ll toss in is Falcons/Steelers. The Falcons are in interesting team on paper. The Steelers are always interesting. We’ll look to see what post-injury Cousins looks like in a real game, and what Russell Wilson looks like in a new place.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Given that the New England Patriots ended up trading Matthew Judon - arguably their best player - for a draft pick anyway, shouldn’t the Patriots have tried to trade more of their veterans for draft picks or young prospects rather than extend them?
Answer: I’ll begin with full disclosure - I’m not a Patriots fan or follower, so I don’t know how many players the Patriots have extended contracts for. I will say this as a general thought - you have a new coach. You need at least a few veteran players to help guide the team through rough waters. That said, it does make some sense to move on from some players and allow the new coach to build his own team. But they can’t all be first and second year guys. You do need some guys with 4–6 years in the league because you can’t teach experience. Moving Judon was big. You lose a strong veteran presence. But you do two things - you make life better for Judon because you know you’re not going to be in Super Bowl contention for a year or two; and you get younger as well as gaining a 3rd round pick, who one would expect could be a contributor early on. Moving other players might make sense, but let’s get real…. who do the Patriots have that you can get value for? You mentioned yourself that Judon was arguably their best player and what did you get for him? A third. There aren’t many players on that team that you’d get more for, so trading them isn’t really a thing. You simply have to draft better and scour the waiver wire as well as identify strong young free agents to bring in. It’s unfortunate but that’s the hole the Patriots are in.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Which quarterbacks in the NFL do you think Jayden Daniels should study and learn from?
Answer: Every single one of the successful ones. There isn’t a successful QB that a rookie shouldn’t try to study and learn from. Daniels is a unique talent - I think there will be some comparisons to other solid QBs from history. I think he’s a better passer than many, and I think his speed will surprise people. I don’t know that he’s as fast as Lamar Jackson or Michael Vick, but he’s plenty quick. And I think even as a rookie he’s a more polished passer than either of them coming out. Lamar has worked hard to improve his passing and it showed up last season. I think Daniels is coming in with more passing skills. I’d prefer him to use his arm over his legs, as the most successful QBs thus far - the championship winners - have been passers first. Mahomes can scramble, but he’s not a runner. I think that would be a good one to emulate. That said, I still think that Daniels will be best served to use his mobility as well. I think in the current game, Lamar and Josh Allen are good models, though I think Daniels is a more polished passer already. Maybe from the old school someone like a Steve Young who was a good scrambler. I’d prefer Daniels not to be seen as a Randall Cunningham type runner, but every time I see Daniels run, I think of Randall Cunningham. They are the exact same body types and size. I’d like for him to be a more accurate passer than Cunningham, and run less frequently, but Cunningham’s elusiveness would serve Daniels well.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What do you think of Tiger Woods' assertion that the Old Course at St. Andrews has become "pretty easy" for big hitters?
Answer: The old course measures 6,721 yards. The average PGA Tour course is 7,344 yards. So basically that’s a 600 yard difference. Right off, that’s a HUGE number. The Old Course was designed for certain shots - shots players no longer take. Players routinely play past the trouble the course was designed with. The quirkiness of the course’s routing and the odd bounces are it’s main defense today, beyond the wind and weather that sometimes pops up. But playing it as it’s laid out, it’s absolutely fairly easy for big hitters. Since Tiger Woods won at St. Andrews in 2000, in the four other Opens contested at St. Andrews, the winning score has been no higher than -14. That includes the -20 shot by Cameron Smith in 2022. And Smith isn’t known as a long hitter; nor were Zach Johnson and Louis Oosthuizen who also won there. If even the short knockers are going low, it’s likely not distance that’s the issue. EDIT: They’ve found a way for tournament play to lengthen the Old Course to 7300 yards, so it’s up to tour average. I didn’t see that in my original reading. The other reason it’s not a tough a course is because of the fact that the course has been relatively reversed since it’s inception. The first hole used to play to what is now the 17th green. Some of the bunkering on the course is odd today, but makes sense when you see the layout as it was originally played and designed to be played. The green of number one was originally the green of the 17th hole, and the tee of the current second hole was the tee of the 18th hole originally - yes, those holes crossed paths.

Question: What positions can switch from offense to defense but not defense to offense (e.g., quarterbacks can never be safeties)?
Answer: When you are young, you play whatever positions the coaches ask you to. It’s not typically until high school football that you start ferreting out which positions a player is best at. Depending on the size of the high school and the number of players on the team, it may simply be impossible to not have many players play both offense and defense. So often position players simply flip from offense to defense seasmlessly. Offensive guards and tackles become defensive linemen, tight ends may be defensive ends or linebackers, and receivers and running backs become defensive backs. In some cases, QBs might be safeties or coernerbacks. Most teams would prefer their QB only play QB to make sure they don’t get hurt. But sometimes the QB is the best athlete on the team. And there are also situations where the QB’s primary position is as a DB - they simply play QB because they’re great athletes.

Question: Should the NFL play more international games? Should they go to 18 games and each team play 2 international games?

Question: Rather than offering guaranteed contracts that pay out regardless of performance - which means that mediocrities such as Daniel Jones become some of the highest paid players in history - why don’t NFL teams offer highly incentive-laden contracts?
Answer: Exhibit A - Ricky Williams. Williams’ first contract was procured by an agency led by rap mogul Master P. It was an incentive laden contract, but the incentives would have been nearly impossible to reach by even the best RBs in history. It’s a dumb deal. He hit almost none of the marks and ended up playing for basically league minimum for much of his time in New Orleans. Look, Sam. I know you’re having an issue with the contracts. I see so many questions you ask about them. Here is the reality. TV is paying oodles of money to the NFL to show games. Insane money, $110 BILLION over 10 years. This is where the players get paid from (contrary to many fans belief that their ticket money pays the players… it doesn’t…). The NFLPA has set certain parameters for players salaries. The cap is a negotiated number that is a percentage of this TV money. So this isn’t a secret to the owners that they’ll pay this percentage to players. That money is pre-negotiated, so it MUST be spent. Play along with me though - let’s say it wasn’t pre-negotiated. You’d be OK with the owners taking the lion’s share of that $110 BILLION, simply for owning the team (note that the owners DO take a HUGE portion of that already… they are one person or relatively small ownership group, while the team splits their money amongst the players)? It’s not fair in our world. We get paid on production, not on future production or due to some arbitrary funding, that increases annually. Closest we get is contracts that say if we get a job done under a certain timeline, we get more money. So we try - erroneously - to apply what works in our world to the world of entertainment and sports. It’s just not that way. Most contracts do have incentives so that you make more for production. But no contract is simply going to be league minimum or base rate and then you get paid for extra production. You may want it to be that way, you may disagree with it, but it’s simply not going to be that way. As long as there are exorbitant TV deals, there will be overpaying of mediocre talent.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What was it like to be in New Orleans during Hurricane Katrina of 2005?
Answer: Like many of the other respondents here, I evacuated. I work in the French Quarter and we were open on the Saturday before the storm hit. Never have I seen such an uneasy feeling around the Quarter. Only about half the bars and restaurants were open, choosing to close and allow their people to evacuate. We were only open until around 2am, as the crowds were very light, for obvious reason. Got home and started watching the news, trying to decide whether to stay or leave. I live in a suburb of New Orleans, across the Mississippi River, which isn’t prone to flooding. Still, the danger was evident. Sunday morning, I decided to leave. Packed up a bunch of stuff and fortunately had a place to go with relatives in northern Louisiana. What is normally about a 4 hour trip took 13 hours in the gridlocked traffic. Arrived at 1am, when the storm just started to hit where we’d left. Watched the news all night and all the next day. It was interesting because as the news signed off on Monday evening, they were commenting on rising water and they didn’t know it’s origin. It’s one thing to watch a disaster happen in places you aren’t familiar with. It’s something else altogether to watch it happen at your home and know that you’re powerless to do anything; and to know that people you know are devastated. We weren’t allowed back into the region for days. Finally about a week after the storm, they allowed certain people into certain areas. There was still flood water in the city, so you couldn’t return to much of the city. But for those of us in outside areas, they allowed us to return over a period of 2–3 days, based on the number on your license plate so as to not have too many people there at once. You were only allowed a certain amount of time, as there was a curfew in place. It was basically grab and go - go assess your damage, salvage what you could, and then leave. I went and emptied my fridge and freezers, packed up long term clothing, and left again, having no idea when I’d get to go home. The thing that struck me about coming in for that day was the same thing others have commented on - the silence. We are used to, in this world, consistent and constant noise. Even if it’s just a hum of some type, there is noise. There was no sound. No dogs barking, no kids playing, obviously no electrical hum. No one had returned with their generators, and even if you had, there was nowhere to get gas for about 30 miles in any direction. It as just eerie silent. Every sound was unusual. Went back to my aunt’s home for a day, then left and went to my future mother in law’s home in South Florida, where we stayed for a month. Power came back on after a month, and we were displaced a total of about 6 weeks. We were very fortunate - no loss, minimal damage, family was healthy and accounted for.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: I am currently in 10th grade. I am a 185 pound 5'11 linebacker in high school and I run a 5.8 40 yard dash. Do I have the ideal size for American football?
Answer: First off, there is no such thing as the “ideal” size. Linebackers have played at smaller and larger statures than yours. What matters is if you can play the game… For a high school sophomore, you’re a solid guy. 5′11″ and 185 is sizeable, and knowing you’re still in growing years, you will get a few inches taller and maybe can put on a few pounds. So size wise, you’re good football size; taller than many of your peers, heavier than many as well. Where you need to work is your foot speed. Unfortunately, a 5.8 isn’t a strong 40-yard time. Even at your age, most of your peers would be faster. You can absolutely take some time off of that - you need to work a ton on foot speed drills and get your speed up. When you are in the 5.0 range, you’ll be cooking for your age. Reality is you should strive to knock a full second off that 40 time. When you get there, you’ll be at the average for a LB. Also remember 40 times aren’t the end all/be all of speed or football. There are a lot of guys who don’t have top straight line speed but have great field speed. Closing gaps and attacking holes, lateral mobility and speed, and good changes of direction are better hallmarks of football speed.

Question: Do American football players at wide receiver position have to only worry about the defensive players guarding them or the whole defense?
Answer: Typically wide receivers are keyed on the person guarding them. They have enough to deal with trying to evade their cover guy. It could be that they have 2 keys, maybe a cornerback and a safety, or a corner and a LB. They might need to have a concept of whether the defense is man or zone. In a zone defense there are soft spots to sit in giving your QB an easy target. In that sense, knowing the whole defense makes a difference. But when running a route in man to man coverage, it’s not common for a WR to need to know more than 2 positions on defense. They need to see how their man is guarding them, and they need to know if that defender has safety help and where that help may come from.

Question: What does someone have to exactly do to get a job as a coach for elementary, middle, and high school athletes, college athletes, and/or professional athletes?
Answer: You are not a human…. LOL. There is no definitive answer to that. Different schools have different requirements, so what you’d have to do to get a job will differ in different places. For most public school districts, in order to be a coach on the staff and get paid, you must be an employee of the school system, which means you’ll have to have at least a college degree. You’ll likely have to teach some subject in some school - maybe not the school you coach at, but somewhere. You’ll need some certification as an educator. Past that, everything varies. You can “coach” outside of the school system, you can be a tutor of sorts. You can coach travel ball or summer leagues without any certification. You can work for or even own a studio or gym where you coach athletes. For college coaching, as a head coach, typically a college degree is required. I’m not positive on assistant coaches. For professional athletes, againas a trainer you can coach anyone anytime. It’s always beneficial to have some formal training to work with athletes, but not required. As for coaching in the pros, you just have to be able to do the job.

Question: Is it worth taking golf lessons from a course pro?
Answer: 100%, assuming you’re going to be a willing student, and the course pro is reputable. First, while there are plenty of folks out there who can teach golf, finding a person who is a PGA of America certified teaching professional is the way to go. These folks go to school to understand HOW to teach. There are a bunch of folks who are good golfers who “teach” but they don’t have the knowledge of how to educate. Imagine going to school where a brilliant person is the teacher but despite all their knowledge has no instruction acumen. Could be difficult. That’s the difference with a PGA professional. But know this - not all PGA pros are made equal. They are all human and differ from one another. It’s OK to shop around and find a person whose teaching style and personality works with yours. That said, taking lessons is the cheat code to better play. When you take a lesson, you’ll work on specific things that are tailored to you exactly. You can find things in books and videos, but until a person has you in front of them and can see your body move in space, you’re not getting a lesson with you in mind. I’ve taken a good few lessons over the years, all from PGA pros. They have every one been insightful and educational. I always take a few things away from them. I don’t practice enough to be great, but the knowledge is invaluable.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do you think J.J. McCarthy will become a starting quarterback this season?
Answer: Still too early to say. His injury nearly completely ensures he won’t be the starter as the season opens. He’s having surgery to repair some meniscus. Time will tell if that’s a short recovery or a longer one; we won’t know until after the surgery how much work needed to be done. It’s going to be hard then, barring a Darnold injury, to see McCarthy recovering and then doing so much in practice to overtake Darnold, particularly since his reps will be limited in number and limited to mostly with the second teamers. Unless the procedure he’s having allows him to resume practice before September, it’s not likely that he is any early thought as the starter. And Darnold would have to struggle mightily or get injured at that point to be replaced. Unfortunately for him, Darnold’s procedure probably locked him into a full season backup role. Exception would be if he’s healthy and the Vikings are in a blowout game and Mccarthy goes in and does well and creates a bit of controversy.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do you think the members of the 2016 Atlanta Falcons psychologically deal with their heartbreaking memory of blowing a 28-3 lead in Super Bowl 51?
Answer: LOL! As a Saints fan, I can’t see or hear this enough! Don’t know if you’re a Saints fan also, or trolling the Falcons, but I’m here for it. Look, it’s sports. You win some, you lose some. Even Brady lost 3 Super Bowls, including two to and obviously lesser team (the NY Giants). And sometimes, you lose in a miserable fashion, as happened to the Falcons. But remember, this isn’t like - say - the Olympics where this comes up once every 4 years. This is the NFL, its your every day, every season career. You are hurt for a while after the game. You deal with the things that went wrong mentally. And then you flush it. After the game, there was no team activity beyond clearing out lockers. The players dispersed for home and the off-season. They went two months before any of them came together for any major partial team activity. As an athlete you know soul crushing losses can happen. And you can’t ever mentally prepare for them. But you have no choice but to psychologically move on. That’s it - that’s the story. Move on. The psychological game you play with yourself is reminding yourself you have next season to atone for that massive failure.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Does an NFL player without a guaranteed contract get paid for the season if he receives a season ending injury in the pre-season?
Answer: Without gurantees in writing, nothing is guaranteed. So no, non-guaranteed monies aren’t paid without some verbal agreement with the team. Not many contracts don’t have at least some guaranteed money, or there is some signing bonus to offset making “nothing”. But yeah, an injury while on a contract with no guaranteed money could be a very big deal for players.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Realistically, can someone who never played football, understands it and is dedicated enough, make the NFL while being a sophomore in college?
Answer: Realistically, absolutley not. Realistically if you haven’t trained and prepared yourself physically, taken the live reps and done the actual work, you have a nearly zero chance of playing football as a college sophomore. For that matter, you’d have a nearly impossible time at most large high schools as a high school senior. Questions like this seem to fail to see the actual work put in even in high schools, particularly the ones that develop college players. It’s not an accident and it’s not something you just pick up. You can know all the rules, you can know plays and play calls but until you’ve physically taken thousands of reps and hits, you’re not prepared. The once exception I always give - special teams. If you’re a kicker or punter (or long snapper for that matter), you may be able to find a spot simply because those positions are highly specialized and it’s tougher to find those players. Kicking is a specific skill. There are guys in the NFL who never played American football before college, some not before the NFL, and they get a shot because they can do something few can - kick a football 65 yards, or punt a ball very high and have it land in a certain area.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Given the inordinately high increases in the salaries of NFL quarterbacks relative to other NFL positions (e.g. running back), are youth players increasingly trying to shifting their skillsets to become quarterbacks?
Answer: I think young players are playing the positions that best fit their personal skill sets. Particularly when you get beyond Pop Warner, you’ll have started to develop certain skills and traits that will be seen by coaches and that will determine your position. I’m certain that some players may attempt to try and develop themselves in other spots. A strong RB may develop better ball skills and try their hand at safety, for example. QB is such a particular and specific position, it’s not really for everyone. Plus there’s only one starting QB on every team. You’re going to expand your opportunity playing any other postion (except center) since there are multiple players at all the other positions. And there’s one more thing - it’s highly unlikely that at the youth ball level you’re focusing on NFL thoughts. I can’t imagine being 9–12 years old having some unrealistic thought about your child playing in the NFL. It’s just so unlikely that it makes no sense for that thought to dictate where you play.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why do many NFL agents and pundits persist in announcing the *total* value of free agent contracts given that savvy observers understand that much (often times most) of that contract value is usually not guaranteed and hence will never be paid out?
Answer: It’s not just agents and pundits - the teams and players want this too. For the agents, it’s advertising and marketing; I’m getting my guys top dollar. Pundits just throw up numbers to catch eyes and get higher ratings. But teams want outside players to know that they are paying big money for their best players. They want to be known as the organization that takes care of their guys, so when players are free agents, they want to come there. And what player doesn’t want to flaunt the idea that they are among the top paid at their spot? So it’s everyone wanting that total value announced. And honestly, it doesn’t matter - yeah, we all know that they may never get the full amount of that contract. The agent knows it, the pundits know it, the players know it, the team knows it. Even most fans know it. It’s not the point. The point is there is the potential to get that. And that’s what the NFL is all about anyway - potential. You don’t sign players solely on what they’ve done - you sign them largely on what you expect them to do. And this is also the big reason for the delays in signing players these days - the squabble over guaranteed money. Because for so long gaudy numbers were assigned but never achieved, players and agents now are equally about guaranteed money on deals as they are big number deals. It’s why the second thing you’ll often hear after you hear the potential contract number is the guaranteed number. For example, Harrison Butker just signed a new deal with the Chiefs. His deal was announced as 4 years, $25.6 million with $17.75 guaranteed. The fact that they average out the salary over time is only for comparison purposes - no one gets that mythical average money every year. Butker will absolutely receive $17.75 million, just short of $8 million less than the overall contract states. If he hits all his markers, he will receive all $25.6 million. But outside of getting booted out of the league or retiring, all of that $17.75 will come to him. The guaranteed money is where it’s at these days and is the most important number. That guaranteed money is what players are more in for today. More and more of the contracts’ values are guaranteed today than ever before.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How will Josh Downs' injury affect the Colts' offense?
Answer: It depends on how long he’s out. Currently they say 4–6 weeks. The season starts in 4 weeks. If he’s on the short end, then the only effect is Downs getting more reps in practice with Richardson between now and opening day. Negative is we all know that high ankle sprains can linger. It could be a full 6 weeks and/or could be a thing that affects him all season. That’s the negative of a high ankle. He could miss no games, he could miss 2 games, he could miss a month of the regular season. We just don’t know. All we can say at this point is it certainly hampers the preparation for the season.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do running backs suffer the brunt of the NFL collective bargaining agreement limiting rookie contract pay given that running backs tend to have such short NFL careers that by the end of their rookie contracts, their careers are probably over anyway?
Answer: In a word, yes. The evolution of the game has made a larger difference, but even through history, RB’s were fairly well done by the time they hit 30. Now, with the passing game being a bigger deal, unless you have a RB who fits well in the passing game, they are simply replaceable after their rookie deals are up; most of them even before that. They absolutely suffer in the CBA limiting rookie deals. Every other position, though, benefits; so RB’s are kind of just out of luck in this scenario.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do most New Orleans police officers lean politically?
Answer: No earthly idea why this is any issue whatsoever. Their political leanings mean ZERO as to doing their jobs of keeping our society safe. You want to find out? Name: Tony Twillie
Question: With the extreme improvements in equipment and training regimens can you honestly compare the athletes from the past with today's athletes?
Answer: I think comparisons over time are next to impossible. And that’s across the board in all sports. Today’s athletes are much more fine tuned because they have the advantage of technology and time. Not only time to work on task, but time that has elapsed over the years which allows them the knowledge of how best to train. Even looking a few decades back - we always thought static stretching was the best method. Not many people do static stretching anymore, at least not as primary stretching. We used to do the hurdler’s stretch - they don’t even allow people to do that stretch much anymore. Point is we evolve. We learn. Back in the 1950’s all the training they did was advanced compared to 1910. That would be the same today as saying what we do today is advanced compared to 1984. And it is. So it makes for impossible comparisons. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Babe Ruth never had to compete in the MLB against black and Latino players. Otto Graham’s offenses were worlds different from Tom Brady’s. We can speculate on how players of the past might have fared today, or how today’s players may have performed in the distant past, but the reality is we just don’t really know.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why didn’t anyone tell NFL star Chad Johnson that “ocho cinco” just means “eight five” in Spanish? (eighty-five would be ochenta y cinco)
Answer: I don’t know Chad Johnson personally, so this is all speculative. But I’d like to venture a very large guess that he knew perfectly well that ocho cinco is eight five literally. Many players will refer to their individual numbers instead of the full number their numerals represent. Literally, an eight and a five are just that - two numbers. It’s only our representation that puts them together as eighty-five. He chose to represent himself in numerals instead of a number. In fact, you never hear him represent himself as “ocho cinco/eighty-five” together, only ocho cinco. So he’s not making any move to say they are one and the same.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Was current Atlanta Falcons head coach, Arthur Smith's anger at New Orleans Saints HC, Dennis Allen, justified after Allen allowed the Saints to score a final minutes touchdown in the 2023 NFL Season ending 48-17 blowout of the Falcons by the Saints?
Answer: First, let’s be clear. Allen didn’t “allow” the Saints to score. The Falcons’ defense allowed the Saints to score. Second, the play wasn’t Allen’s call - Jameis Winston was in at QB and Jamaal Williams was the RB. Williams had scored 17 TD’s in 2022, but had zero coming into the last game of 2023. The offensive unit, led by Winston, decided to get Williams at least one TD for the season. So instead of lining up in victory formation, they lined up in regular formation and ran a play. Let’s be honest - it’s not necessarily the most sporting play. And if victory formation was called, then it’s insubordination. But it was insubordination by a player who knew full well that he wasn’t going to return for another season. Doesn’t make it “right” but it gives perspective. Finally, Arthur Smith was a dead man walking before the Saints kicked him. Is his anger justified? Meh, probably in the small picture. In the big picture, it was kind of a punctuation mark on a bad tenure as head coach. His team stunk, he wasn’t successful. No, it wasn’t the right thing for the Saints to do. That said, I call BS on Allen trying to apologize so profusely to Smith for it. Walk over and say hey, players called that for their guy, not my call. And if Smith balks, tell him to play better defense next time and walk off. And if you ever want your players to have your back again, don’t apologize for them and chastize them in the post game presser, Dennis Allen…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How does Aaron Rogers compare to Peyton Manning and Tom Brady as leaders?
Answer: I feel like their leadership styles are all different. Manning was like a coach - here’s what you need to do and where I’m going to be and this defender is going to do this and we’re going to get this done like this. Brady was more stealth - I’m doing this, all I need you to do is this. Get on my coattails. Rodgers shows up - have you learned this yet? No, I’ll be out back doing ayahuasca until you learn it. Then once you’ve got it, I’ll put my twist on it. Manning seems involved in every step. Brady seems involved in that he’s going to give you some direction. Rodgers seems to just show up and hope you know your job. Anyone who can’t be bothered to show up for workouts or who just doesn’t get much involved until he needs to isn’t really much a leader. Put another way - Manning will be the guy who not only sees the mess, but helps you understand how the mess got there, what the proper execution of using the broom and dust pan is, and will show you how to use them, plus maybe throw in some mopping as well. He’ll do it with you. Brady will bring the dust pan to the mess and put you in the right position to clean it up. Rodgers barely knows where the broom closet is. He’s one of the best at getting the job done, but he’s going to show up, show you where to sweep, leave you to go date a supermodel or racecar driver or an actress, come back to see how you’ve done, critique what you’ve done, leave again to go on a retreat, then return and if you’re not done, he’ll pout.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why would the Saints draft RT/of Fuaga over Fautanu or Mims if they knew they needed a left tackle?
Answer: Question mark on Mims…. Mims is a right tackle also, so that wouldn’t put them any different. Fautanu wasn’t graded as highly on most boards as Fuaga. The higher grade typically means a better overall skill set, so moving Fuaga was potentially going to be easier than Mims, and if he’s already a better player than Fautanu, then why not take that shot? Once you got past Alt, Latham, and Fashanu, it was going to be rolling the dice any way you slice it. There wasn’t another left tackle with nearly the skills of those three guys. So it made sense to at least take the next best tackle on the board and move him over taking a lesser tackle and hoping he worked out. We already tried that with Penning…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do people hate New Orleans Saints fans? Why or why not?
Answer: I’m a New Orleans Saints fan, so I’m answering from the inside out. Here’s what happens when an opposing fan comes to New Orleans. First, they are treated to a getaway in a truly unique city; one unlike any other in the US. It’s almost a Caribbean devil-may-care vibe. They can partake in the fun of the French Quarter or Frenchman Street, they will eat at some of the best restaurants in the country. They may visit a national museum dedicated to WWII. New Orleans is a perfect weekend city because it’s small enough that you can see and do a lot in just one weekend. You’ll head to the game on Sunday. You’ll be clowned with by people tailgating with loud music in nearby parking lots. If you clown back, they’ll laugh and likely invite you over for some jambalaya or BBQ. If it’s winter and it’s cold, they may even have gumbo. And if they do, trust me, it will be better than the gumbo in 90% of the restaurants in town. You’ll sit in the Superdome and unless you’re in a large group of loud, rowdy, raucous fans of your team, you’re likely to spark up a conversation with folks around you from here. They’ll ask where you’re from and how you’re enjoying the city. They’ll tell you were to go get great food postgame. And they might even invite you to come with them postgame to a few spots they’d like to hit for drinks. New Orleans doesn’t do pretension. We’re having a good time. You came here because you wanted to have a good time. That’s enough for us. This is the city where celebrities come to hide in plain sight. Our fans are loyal to the Saints and you’re not going to put them down. WE can (and will on occasion) talk bad about them, but you can’t. As long as you’re not coming in with guns blazing talking trash, you’re not going to be accosted by a Saints fan. Every year, I see at least one altercation in the stands, and it’s usually a fan - inebriated - who is in their team’s jersey and who has taken it upon themselves to tell Saints fans where they can go. And usually, it’s that fan who ends up going with NOPD “escorts”. To the contrary - I went to a game in Seattle and was just rudely harassed by several fans on the way to the stadium, in the stadium, and on the way from the stadium. It was a lot. I’ve also been to Miami and while most of the fans were very laid back, one guy kept riding me. He sat next to me, seeming to be looking for big reaction from me. As the Saints fell behind, he got more boisterous and obnoxious. When the Saints came from behind, I said nothing; I just kept looking at him with every TD we scored, until we went up by 2 scores and he got up and left. And when he did, the other fans around us were kind of thankful because they were embarrassed by him. And I’ve been to two Saints/Tampa Bay games in Tampa, but those were different because Tampa was a bad team at the time and their fans didn’t much show up for games. The first one I went to, Saints fans were nearly equal in number to Tampa fans. PLEASE come to New Orleans for your team’s game against the Saints.

Question: In September, 3 of the Tampa Bay Bucs first 4 games will be at home. The temps are regularly in the 90's during that month. Why doesn't the NFL schedule more home games in the North during that time and later on, in the south?

But it’s at least a slight advantage to you.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What would be the impact on Louisiana if Trump is elected president as opposed to Harris?

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What happens when a golf ball lands in water?
Answer: It gets wet… From a golf standpoint, it depends on the water it lands in. If it has rained, often the tournament or course committee allows for moving balls from what is called casual water - water that has formed on the course that may pool in lower lying areas. If your ball is in casual water and the committee is allowing for ball in hand, that means you may lift, clean, and place your ball in an area that doesn’t have standing water or water pooling up around your ball or feet as you take your stance. It’s a free relief situation, no closer to the hole. Beyond that, if you ball is in a marked (water) hazard, you have several options. If the hazard is marked with yellow stakes (typically seen when the water is a pond between the golfer and the green, or if there is room on the other side of the hazard in the typical line of play), you have 4 options - 1. Play the ball as it lies, no penalty; 2, go to the point where the ball last crossed the margin of the hazard and drop on a line extending backwards away from the hole keeping that point and the hole in line, within 2-clublengths of the hazard, with a one stroke penalty; 3, drop a ball on that same line any distance back from the point at which the ball crossed the hazard, with a one stroke penalty; 4, drop another ball as near the spot you just hit from and play your next shot from that spot, with a one stroke penalty. For a red-staked hazard (which is typically a hazard that is parallel to the typical line of play), you have two more options. 1, you may go to that point where the ball last crossed the margin of the hazard and drop a ball within two clublengths of that spot, no nearer to the hole, and play your subsequent shot from there, with a one stroke penalty; 2, you may go to the other side of the hazard, and - keeping that point where the ball last crossed the margin as a reference - on a line back from that spot on the other side, drop a ball any distance back, keeping that point and the hole aligned, with a one stroke penalty. But my real answer is when the ball goes in the water I say grown-up words, or I cry a bit…

Question: How is it that Devon Hester is just now entering the National Football Hall of Fame?

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Who's more athletic in their prime, Bo Jackson or DK Metcalf?
Answer: You will absolutely not find a person who has ever seen Bo Jackson play believe that they’ve seen a superior overall athlete in their lives. Bo was just unique. DK is a hoss, for sure. But Bo was from another planet athletically. He did things that still haven’t been replicated…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is being a professional quarterback considered a difficult position compared to other positions in football, such as offensive line, defensive line, and linebackers?
Answer: YES. Every position in football is important and difficult. There are a ton of what if scenarios for every spot. But there are only 2 positions on every snap of the offensive game that are guaranteed to touch the football - center and QB. The QB is expected to understand not only everything he has to do, but everything every other offensive play has to do; and much of what the defense will be trying to do as well. Even if it’s something as simple as a handoff - the offensive line has to know who their blocking assignments are and where the play is designed to go. The QB has to know that, plus understand where the RB is going to take the handoff, where the options may be, what the defense has shown in regards to the success of that play…. There are just a myriad things for the QB to know and check.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do NFL teams prepare for a game?
Answer: Assuming a Sunday game… Monday - go to team facilities in the morning and get a workout in, plus begin rehab on any injuries suffered in Sunday’s game. Review film of the previous game. Maybe team/group meetings. Tuesday - typically a player’s day off. This is the day they will often do things with their family, or do charitable work. Coaches will be in the team facility prepping the new game plan; continuing reviewing film of the upcoming opponent - after they digest the previous game’s film, the quickly begin planning for Sunday’s game on Monday evening, into Tuesday. Wednesday - install of the game plan for the following weekend begins. Some teams break things down in different ways, but often they’ll install first and second down on Wednesday. There will be tons of positional meetings, side meetings (offense/defense/special teams), and team meetings all day around the walkthrough/practice. Thursday - much of the same - maybe it will be third down and 4th down and red zone install on Thursday. Lots of meetings. Friday - lighter practice, full review of installs from Wed and Thurs, plus special teams. More meetings. Saturday - morning walk through practice, no contact. More meetings. If you’re the road team, you go home and then reconvene to fly out to visiting team site. Some home teams will have the team meet at a local hotel, so they can keep tabs on them overnight and continue to have meetings. Travel or home, there will be meetings into the evening, potentially even hotel walk throughs. Sunday morning - meet for breakfast together. Home team may or may not convene in this way, depending on the team and coaches. But if a team is doing a hotel stay, they will get together in the morning for breakfast and potentially have a final walk through. They will head over to the stadium a few hours before the game and beging warm ups and game day prep. That will be light catching and throwing, stretching, conditioning drills, getting taped up. After that, teams go and get dressed and come out for organized drills. This is team stretching and then team drills at half speed. They return to the locker rooms for any last updates or changes, then get ready for introductions.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Does Tiger Woods have his $1.3 billion all in cash?
Answer: Most people who have high personal self worth do not have much of their money in cash. Tiger Woods is no exception. Personal net worth is a formula - assests (cash, stock holdings, real estate, net worth of businesses, other items of value - cars, boats, art) minus liabilities (debts, monies owed). We have no idea how much cash Tiger has on hand. But we know his Jupiter Island home is worth between $50 and $80 million. And he has a $20 million yacht as well. All these things would be part of his portfolio of wealth. So that would be at the very least a $100 million start of his net worth not being liquid cash.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do you think Taysom Hill's role will change in the New Orleans Saints' offense under offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak?
Answer: I think the emphasis on him being a rushing QB taking direct snaps from the center will be curtailed, or at least lessened. Question: How many golf courses are named after President Trump?
Answer: None. Named after is an honor. When someone does something or has a certain position, something may be named after them. George Bush International Airport, for example, is named after someone. Every place in the US that has Washington in it is named after someone. Trump simply places his name on things because it’s supposed to connote a certail level of prestige. Different from named after; there isn’t any honor to it. While his name is associated with 17 courses worldwide, he only built a handful of those - most of them were purchased and he just placed his name on them - Turnberry and Doral are good examples of that. But there are no courses named in honor of him.

Question: Who were the best defensive players on the 1985 Chicago Bears?
Answer: The most popular star of that defense was Mike Singletary. He was maybe the biggest name on that D, since linebackers get a ton of love typically. But make no mistake that defense was riddled with some of the best defenders of the decade. Richard Dent was an offense wrecker. He’s on a list of all-time greats as a HOFer. He had 17 sacks that season and may have been the absolute best player on the defense that year. On the back end, Dave Duerson was their big name DB. He had a couple of sacks as well as 5 interceptions that season. But some may recall that another person whose name maybe became bigger as a coach had 6 picks that season for the Bears - Leslie Frazier. And free safety Gary Fencik wasn’t a slouch either. Otis Wilson might have been the best linebacker that season. Tackles weren’t counted as an official stat at that time, but Wilsond did have 10.5 sacks and 3 interceptions, including one returned for a TD. Singletary may have out-tackled him, but Wilson was absolutely a beast. The best of the best that year in my opinion was Dent. Wilson, Hampton, McMichael, Duerson, Marshall, and obviously Singletary as the leader of the D were all stellar. Hard to say who were the best when the entire collection of defenders were great.

Question: Since when did you first start playing golf and do you still play?
Answer: I’m far different than most here… I played multiple sports in high school and was good enough to walk on and make a college baseball team. Baseball playing ended abruptly and I transitioned to coaching baseball. On my 21st birthday, two of my assistant coaches were going to play, as well as one of my players (I was coaching high school summer ball so the team still had players I’d played with on the team) and asked me to be their fourth. Mind you, my golf experience was hitting balls at the range once with some other baseball teammates just for fun and to try and see how far we could hit them. I stunk. So I was 21 in 1988 when I started. We played 9 holes, the back nine at one of local courses because they had a scramble on the front nine on Thursday afternoons. I hit them everywhere. Some swings and misses, some shanks, some hooks. Hard to immediately transfer a baseball swing into a golf swing. Then on the 18th hole, I hit the purest 3 wood onto the green. Long and straight. That was the shot that hooked me. I went back out a few more times that summer, then bought my own golf clubs soon after that. Yes, I still play. Sadly, my handicap is higher than it should be for a person who’s played as long as I have and as much golf as I have. I have moments when I’m pretty good and shoot in the lower 80’s, and then days when nothing is right and I’m taking a ton of penalty strokes and shoot triple digits. But my typical score is bogey golf. Sadly, I’m just not interested in doing the extra work to get better - all the practice.

Question: Why could it be a little bit dated and childish for a pitcher to hit a batter in the back after they gave up a homerun?
Answer: I don’t know that this statement tells the entire story; because this isn’t really a thing. Batters hit home runs all the time. Pitchers give up home runs all the time. It’s not a reason to hit a batter by itself. Now - if you hit that home run and you stand at the plate admiring it until it’s out of the ballpark; or you hit it and do some kind of celebration; or you hit it and you have something to say to the pitcher or the opposing team about it; or it takes you 35–40 seconds to round the bases… then yeah - you can expect to wear a baseball next time around because you earned that yourself. And even the standing there admiring it has layers. You bomb one out of the stadium, you’re likely to watch for a bit - that’s not a reason for a clip. That only comes when you are doing something to intentionally show up the opposing team or pitcher. And also remember - throwing at someone’s head isn’t normally an intention to hit them. The head is one of the easier things to move out of the way. If you’re trying to hit a batter, you’ll throw at their torso, which is harder to move out of the way. Throwing high and tight is a purpose pitch - you’re trying to take some plate back. Or you didn’t like something they did and it’s a warning. Hitting a batter puts on a baserunner. In today’s world of metrics, that is always bad. And yes, we are aware that many of baseballs “traditions” are seen as archaic. But sometimes, things have to be handled. Most managers understand the nature of the game. Giving up a homer isn’t a reason for a retaliation pitch. Heck, if I gave up 2 homers, that’s on me throwing bad pitches. I might throw one behind the guy the next time up, just because I want to make him guess, or I don’t want him to hit his next homer on the first pitch. But I’m not hitting them for my error.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why do people cheat at golf?
Answer: Many different reasons: Because they can - Golf is the one sport that relies on self policing. Your ball moves, you have to tell your opponent about it. If your ball is in a place where you have to call a penalty on yourself, it’s up to you. Some people will simply lack the integrity to do the right thing. Becuase no one will know - if you don’t call it on yourself, no one will know that you cheated. Back to the integrity things. Because they’re too competitive - they want to win at all costs. These folks cheat at more than golf. Because they don’t know the rules - and sadly, often the rules can be to your advantage. But they don’t know them so they break them. This is inadvertent cheating, but cheating nonetheless. Status - being a good golfer is a status thing, so often golfers will cheat to achieve a perceived higher standing (untill they play in a competition and people find out they have a vanity handicap…) Better standing - often golfers will cheat to gain an advantage in a field. Known as sandbagging, sometimes golfers will inflate their handicap - whether through throwing away holes or rounds and entering ill-gotten scores, or by simply entering a higher number than they really scored - golfers will use those higher handicaps when playing in future competitions, enabling them to easily score better than their handicap and win or place highly in tournaments. This is but a few reasons people cheat. All of them bad.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why are modern golf balls more difficult to curve?
Answer: Design. Modern golf balls aren’t made the same. Older golf balls were made with rubber banding wound on the interior, wrapped around a solid core (or in some cases, a liquid core). This made for a ball that was easier to turn, they curved a lot when mishit. Todays balls have solid cores and resist excess turning unless you specifically try to make them turn. I don’t know that today’s balls are more difficult to curve. Just relative to the past, slightly less than perfect strikes caused them to curve a lot, and really less than perfect hits cause them to curve immensely. With today’s ball, you need to be more purposeful in making it curve. They can curve, but slightly off center hits won’t be as big a deal anymore.

Question: If someone's a good golfer, should they start playing in amateur tournaments first or go straight into playing against pros?
Answer: Umm… wow. OK, first off, all golf isn’t about competition with others. Often it’s competition within yourself, trying to be the best you can be. Maybe it’s competiton with friends in a club or the members’ tournament at your course. Typically even for pretty good golfers, that’s about where it ends. But lets assume your game is really good and it travels. Amateur tournaments are available both regionally and nationally, all the way up to the US Amateur. But note - US Amateur contestants are typically the very best amateurs. They’re folks whose games are maybe just a step or two behind some mini-tour pros - maybe better than some mini-tour guys. That’s an option you have. But under no circumstances would a person who is a “good golfer” need to play a straight up match with a touring professional golfer. If you think you’d like to become a professional, then you’d start playing major amateur events, then maybe some mini-tours and finally the Korn Ferry Tour which is the AAA affililate of the PGA Tour. The vast majority of mini-tour guys are never going to sniff the PGA Tour. And they are scratch to plus handicap golfers in most cases - they’re professional golfers but they’re not PGA Tour level golfers. So there isn’t any definitive answer to your question, but I’ll say that no regular good golfer is ready to play pros right off.
