Question: Captain Obvious here: If Tom Brady had played his final three seasons in New England, would Bill Belichick now be the winningest coach in NFL history? Are those three lost seasons going to be what prevents Belichick from breaking Don Shula’s record?
Answer: Let’s play pretend… In Brady’s last season with the Pats, they were drug kicking and screaming to wins by him and a solid defense. They had only Edelman as an offensive playmaker. That 12 wins in 2019 was a scheduling gift - the Pats had the easiest schedule in the NFL. If we were to assume the trend of not getting offensive playmakers were to continue, and we could assume their schedule wouldn’t be that easy again, then we can say the liklihood of them winning 12 games would be minuscule. I wouldn’t assume more than 10 wins for them in each of those next 3 seasons. Tampa Bay averaged just under 11 wins in each of the next 3 seasons with a far superior team than New England, so actually giving New England 10 wins even with Brady at QB might be pushing it. You say 3 lost seasons - there is a 7 game differential between what Tampa Bay put up and what New England put up. So let’s give Belichick those 7 games - doubtful they’d have gotten there even with Brady, but it’s in the ballpark - I gave them 30 wins max with Brady in NE, this is 32 wins. That would have put Belichick at 336 wins. That’s still 11 wins behind Shula. Then again, it’s conceivable that despite having Brady’s talent, having so little talent around him hurt them and they only win 9 games a year, putting him at 331 over 3 seasons and being 16 wins behind. IF I calculate correctly, Belichick was at 304 total wins when Brady left? That’s 43 shy of tying Shula. In the time Brady was still active, each team played 50 total games. Let’s be honest - Belichick, nor Brady was winning 14–15 games a season, not with that team and not with any team. Again, assuming a reasonable number considering that team of 10 wins a season and 30 total wins, you’re left with still a very good season’s worth of wins. So no, not in the time of Brady would Belichick have gotten there. Were Brady to stay an extra year or two, then maybe. But at 10 wins a season, it would have taken more than 4 seasons to get there. You’d have to hope for four 11-win seasons. And again, with that team…. not likely.

Question: What are the rules for picking up a golf ball after hitting it off course without losing the hole or taking penalty strokes?
Answer: The rules of golf are very specific about what you may or may not do with your golf ball. If by hitting it “off course” you mean literally OFF the course, like out of bounds (OB), there is no penalty for touching your ball. As it is OB, it cannot be played as it lies, so you may pick it up and clean it if you like. OB is a stroke and distance penalty in competition, so you don’t have the option to play it where it went OB. As souch picking it up isn’t an issue. If by hitting it “off course” you mean within the confines of the course, like you hit it somewhere besides the fairway, different rules apply. If it’s in a water hazard and you do not intend to play it as it lies (some water hazards may be dry or have dry areas…), you may pick it up and clean it, as your intent is to drop it back into play according to the rules of golf, with a stroke penalty assessed. If it is in a hazard (sand trap, for example), or if it is on the ground anywhere else, you may NOT pick up the ball without being assessed a penalty. The exception here would be if your ball interferes with the ball or stance of a fellow competitor. If so, the fellow competitor may ask you to move your ball while they play their shot. IMPORTANT - you must place the ball just as you found it: you may not clean it or alter the orientation of the ball when you replace it in the spot. If you are just picking up A golf ball, as in any ball that is not yours or a fellow competitors, and that ball is in play, you should check all around you to be certain you’re not picking up a ball from a hole - or sometimes several holes - away. Errant shots happen. If you question what a ball is doint sitting in an area, leave it.

Question: Did LSU's star gymnast try out for the Olympic team and not make it? I've seen her and she is absolutely stunning and a great gymnast.
Answer: OK, that could be one of three people… not that there aren’t more than three stunning gymnasts on LSU’s team - there are way more than that. Not that I was paying attention… LOL. Olivia Dunne is the obvious stunner. She’s the one with the ridiculous NIL deals and the huge social media following. She’s also the girlfriend of the NL All-Star starting pitcher Paul Skenes (love being able to say that! Geaux Tigers!). Dunne’s social media and modeling far exceeds her gymnastics. She’s obviously good to be on the National Championship team, but she’s not the best of the LSU gymnasts. Haliegh Bryant IS the best of the LSU gymnasts. She won the All-Around competition in the NCAA finals. She’s a phenomenal gymnast. But there is a gap between collegiate gymnastics and elite world competition gynmastics. To note, our greatest gymnast ever, Simone Biles, never competed in college gymnastics. It’s because world class level gymnastics requires more time and energy than most collegiate gymnasts have to give. College athletics/gymnastics are limited to about 20 hours of practice a week. Some elite gymnasts practice double that amount of time. So while she’s the best collegiate gymnast, she’s not prepared for the longer routines or more intense scrutiny of Olympic gymnastics. Then there are other more unusual cases. LSU gymnast Aleah Finnegan was an elite gymnast until after her freshman year at LSU. She’d been on the US National team but had failed to qualify for the Olympic trials. She was just content to be an LSU gymnast, having given up the grueling demands of elite gymnastics. Then she was contacted by the gymnastics association of the Phillipines - her mother is a Filipino. They asked if she wanted to tryout for their team. She did, and made it, becoming the first female gymnast to represent the Phillipines since 1964. So one LSU gymnast is an Olympian, but not the one you may have thought and not for this country.

Question: Do professional golfers have preferred courses they like to play at? If so, what are some examples?
Answer: Of course they do, just as most humans have courses they prefer. Typically golfers prefer courses that set up in a way that suits their game. Some like them very long because they are longer hitters and it eliminates the shorter hitters. Some like them with tighter doglegs because it forces the long hitters to play uncomfortably. All of them like only moderate rough. They all prefer fluffy sand. On Tour there are courses you’ll see many top golfers look to play because the field will be strong and the test of golf will be challenging but fair. Just off the top of my head, I can think of Bay Hill, Muirfield Village, Quail Hollow, Pebble Beach, St. Andrews, and Riviera. As well every golfer will nod a head to Augusta National. Beyond that, many pros love the courses you’ll see on the world’s top 100 list. Courses they don’t play often, but truly love and respect.

Question: Is it common for star quarterbacks to also play on defense in American football?

Coaches don’t want their star players getting injured needlessly, so they won’t allow QB’s to do anything to increase their chances of injury.

Question: Can you explain the concept of "out of bounds" in golf? Is there a specific rule that determines what is considered outside the boundaries?
Answer: The club’s committee will determine where out of bounds will be set on a course. Typically, if the course lies in a neighborhood, the back property line of the homeowners, whether fenced or not, will constitue the out of bounds line. Any streets that border the property will likewise likely be out of bounds. Typically there is no out of bounds placed along the edge of woods, nor would they be placed on the interior of the course unless the course’s driving range is parallel to play. Out of bounds is anything the committe deems an area that is not part of the course. It will not be maintained by the course. The border of the out of bounds will be designated by a white line running along the ground, or by white stakes placed at varying intervals along the OB, or by fence lines or streets (and typically even streets have white markers of some type along them). The ball is out of bounds when the entire ball lies beyond the outer margin of the hazard line. If any of the ball is within the boundary, the ball is in play. The player may stand out of bounds to hit a ball that is in bounds.

Question: Which song is the most racist, "Try that in a small town" or "rich men north of Richmond"? I know both are racist, but which is worse?

While I don’t necessarily agree with the previous respondents, I do think you should really read the lyrics - and in the case of Aldean’s video, watch the video. I do feel like you’ve taken what you’ve heard and asked a question without actually reading the words to the songs. They’re readily available in many places online.

Question: Is a lost golf ball still considered out of bounds if someone throws it back?
Answer: OK, Quora bot… First things first - there is a difference between a lost ball and a ball out of bounds. A ball can be lost AND out of bounds, but you can have a lost ball on the course as well. Yes, the penalty is the same - stroke and distance - but the adjudication of each is specific. Your ball is lost when you search for 3 minutes after arriving where you assume the ball is and you cannot find it. It is a stroke and distance penalty. You may simply lose your ball in high grass, or in a tree. A lost ball is a ball you don’t find, period. It doesn’t have to be out of bounds. Your ball is out of bounds when it crosses and comes to rest beyond the margin of the out of bounds line. It may be perfectly visible to you, not lost at all, but it is out of the designated course area. Golf is funny, though. Let’s say you’re playing a course that has some tough sightlines. You hit a ball that is headed out of bounds. You’re virtually certain it’s going OB. As you approach the area, you see your ball in play. You’re almost certain it was going OB, but it’s not OB. There is no one there to tell you how it got to that place. That ball would be in play. Even if someone was in their backyard, picked it up and threw it back into play, it’s in play. Unless you or someone else physically saw a person pick the ball up and throw it back into play, you’re not penalized for not knowing how it got back into play. It could have hit a tree, a house, bounced off a trampoline…. any number of ways. And it can hit a tree out of bounds and bounce back into play and be playable - it’s where the ball comes to rest which is important here. HOWEVER, if you hit the ball OB and witness a person pick it up and throw it back onto the course, or you come up and a person tells you it landed and stopped OB and they just tossed it back for you, then you must record it as OB. A person cannot physically assist your ball getting into play. But let’s go another step. A player hits a ball towards the OB line. A spectator is standing on a slope and the ball comes to rest by their foot. If they move, the ball will roll towards OB, likely going out. That spectator may stand there until the golfer arrives and marks the spot. Then the spectator may move, and the golfer can attempt to drop the ball on the spot the ball was at rest, against the spectators foot. If the golfer drops and the ball rolls away towards the OB, the golfer can re-drop. If on the second drop the ball does the same, the golfer may place the ball on the spot of the second drop and then play on, no penalty at all.

Question: What is the difference between using one ball and two balls in golf?
Answer: Oh, Quora-bots…. Such inane questions… You don’t get to use two balls in golf (insert terrible male/dad joke here). You start a hole with one golf ball, you finish the hole with that same golf ball. You may change golf balls if a ball becomes deformed or scuffed, but the concept is to use one golf ball. You don’t get to arbitrarily use one ball to tee off and another for approaches and or putts. I’ve played with golfers who do that - a distance ball off the tee and then a soft spinny ball for approaches and putts. That’s not legal, actually.

Question: What is the process for seasoning an entire pot of water for a Louisiana style seafood boil?
Answer: Everyone’s boil is different, which is part of the beauty of the boil. I have a buddy who boils crawfish that I swear by. I can’t do it like him. And I buy it from a lot of places, but it’s not the same. I don’t do crawfish but I do boil shrimp at home. But the process would be the same. My family doesn’t like all the excess flavors so I try to keep it simple. For my boil, it’s easy. I put my potatoes in the pot when I put my water in. I use the Zatarains bags for flavor, usually 2 bags for the 6–7 pounds I’ll boil for my household. Salt. I’ll cut up 2 lemons and put them in. I’ll also put in the liquid concentrate seafood boil. Usually I’ll boil the water, then add the concentrate later, when I bring it back from a rolling boil. Sometimes I put in actual onion and garlic, and sometimes andouille, but usually I don’t because again, my family isn’t interested in all the flavor. But that’s really it. Once it’s good and ready, which is usually when the potatoes are fork soft, I put the seafood in. For shrimp, the cook time is VERY short. Never more than 2 minutes of cook time. Then you bring them off the heat and cover them and let them soak up the flavor for at least 15 minutes - the longer the better. Some people put ice in to stop the cooking, I do not.

Question: How do the NFL Draft and the Supplemental Draft differ from each other?

Question: How do caddies in the PGA Tour aid in green reading?
Answer: The players themselves are very proficient in reading greens. Caddies are usually there to give their player confidence that what they are seeing is correct. Not all golfers have their caddies assist in reading putts. Typically the caddies do the exact same things the players would. They’ll note grain. They’ll note drainage off the green to know where the ball might pull to. They’ll pay attention to bunkers and things that may affect the ball’s movement on the green. But at the end of the day, only the player themselves pulls the trigger on the putt.

Question: How true is the notion that there is little benefit for a team in just remaining average (e.g. having a .500 W/L record) for years on end, and that such teams are better off trading their best players for draft picks to become a future contender?
Answer: A very nuanced situation, based on many factors. For a team like - say - the New Orleans Saints, being very average for a long time is a big deal, but not a deal breaker. The Saints were very poor in their formative years and remained pretty poor until the mid-1980s. So when they became average and stayed average for years, it was a benefit. As an average team today, it’s tougher because the expectations have been raised through the Drew Brees years. That said, there is still not an empty seat in the house on game day, so while competitively they’re not strong, financially, they’re still improving. This would be the same for teams like Green Bay who have a rabid fan base and a strong following. For some teams in larger markets, while they will survive regardless, they’re going to be more scrutinized for not making moves to be better than average. And for teams in smaller markets like Jacksonville, they must find a way to be competitive or they’ll suffer. But in a general sense, remaining average isn’t a good business model. A team has to balance things though. Trading off strong young talent or marquee names isn’t necessarily the best business model either. You need those strong young players to build the future around. And you may need those marquee names to keep rears in seats. It might make all the sense in the world for Anaheim to have dealt Trout off years ago. But it he’s not there today, would anyone care at all about the Angels? Flip side is if you had moved him in his prime, you might today be reaping the rewards of having brought in some great young talent. That’s why the GMs get paid the big bucks…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do Par 3 golf courses differ from traditional 18-hole courses?
Answer: Par 3 courses are typically created with only holes that are par 3 holes; holes designed for the skilled golfer to get the ball into the hole in 3 strokes. Traditional courses mix par 3 holes with par 4 and par 5 holes, normally four par 3 holes and four par 5 holes, with the other 10 being par 4 holes. On a par 3 course, all 18 holes would be par 3s. Not to say they can’t be difficult… they can mix in par threes well over 200 yards. Usually there will be a solid mix of short, medium, and long par 3 holes.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What are the differences between a soft and hard golf ball? How can you determine which type of ball you have?
Answer: Feel and performance are the biggest differences! Soft balls will feel more spongy off the club, even off of putter facess. They will tend to spin more and land softer. They are also easier to hit in the air. Harder balls will often have a different sound coming off the club, more of a ‘click’ sound. They will feel harder. They tend to spin less and fly lower, land quicker, and will tend to roll out more when they hit the ground. On the shelf, you may see them advertised as “distance” balls. They are also seen as the X balls in some lines, as in the ProV1x and the Chrome Soft X. These are premium balls that tend to be a bit firmer, while retaining many of the qualities of softer balls. Typically when you purchase balls at the store, you’ll see on the packaging which balls you’re getting. Manufacturers do a good job of explaining which type ball you have and are getting. Firmer balls are preferred by golfers who tend to compress the ball a lot. Sometimes people with slower swing speeds also think firm balls are better for them since they’re harder, come off the face of the club quicker, and roll a bit more. But realistically, softer balls will tend to travel more in the air, which is typically more benficial for those with slower swing speeds.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What are the rules for hitting a golf ball into the woods and then searching for it?
Answer: According to the latest rules of golf, you personally (the golfer) have 3 minutes from the time you begin looking in the area you think your ball should be in. Other people may look for the ball for you as well, but the 3 minutes doesn’t start until you begin looking yourself. If you find the ball and it is in bounds, you play it as it lies. If you cannot play it as it lies, you may opt to take a drop to get a clearer shot, under penalty of a stroke (unplayable ball rules). If you cannot find the ball after 3 minutes of searching, you must go back to where you hit your last shot, drop a ball as near as possible to the spot you last hit from and play your next stroke under penalty of one stroke.

Question: After the debate, a video showing Joe Biden's iron shot makes people say, "If he is a 6 handicap (as Biden himself claimed) I'm Tiger Woods." Is or was Biden a 6 hadicap golfer?
Answer: Biden claims to have been an 8 handicap golfer at some point while he was VP. In the debate he said 6, but corrected it to an 8 later. An 8 handicap golfer would shoot around 80 one in every 10 rounds, with a lot of other rounds in the low 80’s. Is that impossible? No it’s not. Is it likely? No it’s not. Not with his swing, not only playing a round or so every couple of weeks. You have to work at your game consistently to keep that type handicap. Not saying Joe doesn’t or didn’t, but his swing is one that you’d have to work a ton at to have a handicap like that. His deal is simple - he never really entered scores very often. It’s possible in his earlier years in the Senate he was an 8 handicap and he just never entered scores showing higher rounds. That’s a vanity handicap. He could never play to that handicap I’d guess in his later VP years, and definitely not today.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do NFL teams typically decide how long their starters will play in preseason games?
Answer: Depends on the team really, and it depends on the players. A veteran starting QB is going to get very little run in the preseason unless he specifically asks for more snaps. But offensive starters are going to play probably no more than a quarter’s worth of time in the preseason, if that. Many starters will play just a few snaps, maybe one full drive. Offensive linemen will play more than that, gaining cohesiveness is important and they spend little time in full contact in preseason. Defensive starters will play a bit more; the chance of injury is still high, but maybe less high than for an offensive player. The caveat is if you have a rookie starter, you may give them more pre-season snaps so they can see more near game speed reps.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: With a 6 handicap in golf, could Biden turn pro?
Answer: Not remotely, unless he was going to teach golf. The Professional Golfers Association of America teach the game, and they do not have to be scratch golfers. He’d have to show that in a proficiency test that the PGA of America administers for competency. As for being a tour pro, no 6 handicap on the planet could be a tour pro on any major tour. Not even Trump with his 2.8 handicap (HAHAHAHA!) made up total of 20 scores he’s entered since 2011 (most golfers enter every round or close to it - how a person who played almost every weekend of their 4 year presidency didn’t have any scores to post is a mystery to me….) would be able to play on even the Champions Tour. Neither of those guys are playing with professional golfers, who all possess plus handicaps.

Question: How would you rank Brock Purdy among starting quarterbacks in the NFL?

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How is it that the AP NFL MVP winner in a year is seldom the same player as the AP Offensive Player of the Year or the AP Defensive Player of the Year? Shouldn’t the most valuable player also be either the best offensive or best defensive player?
Answer: I posted in a reply to another answer, but I’ll place this here too. First, let’s eliminate defensive player of the year. As posted in Frank Cuzzocrea’s response, the last defensive MVP was Lawrence Taylor. So if Reggie White couldn’t get it, or Ray Lewis, or JJ Watt, or Aaron Donald, then no one else should get it. As the league becomes more offensive, the chances of a defensive player being able to get that award is going the way of the dodo. As for OPY and MVP, the difference is in how they are determined. The difference in OPY and MVP is seen in the names. OPY is the best offensive producer, period - which player’s offensive production was the most outstanding with not much regard to anything else. There, it could be a QB, WR, or RB. Maybe even a TE under odd circumstances. It could be a guy who catches 97 passes for 1,800 yards on a team that goes 8–9. That’s an outstanding player, but his production didn’t help his team be successful, so his value is different. Valuable to that team, yes. More valuable to that team than another player to his team’s success, not necessarily. For MVP, you’re really limited. MVP is (supposed to be) the player whose production was most critical to their team’s success. In some cases, that may be the same person as the OPY, but you can have a person who has outstanding offensive production but their team isn’t very outstanding. Their value is great, but may not be as valuable as a person who had maybe slightly lesser numbers but whose production led to greater things. Or, for a team who didn’t do as well, but without that player’s production the team would have been much poorer. Usually its a QB because we see annually that teams who trot out a backup QB struggle to do as well. The Carson Wentz-Nick Foles days are typically an aberration - you’re more likely to get performances like Aaron Rodgers-Zach Wilson, or Kirk Cousins-Josh Dobbs-Nick Mullens-Jared Hall. The fall-off is more pronounced in the QB ranks than any other position, which signifies the QB’s value to the team.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do professional golfers use long drivers or do they all use regular drivers and adjust their swing?
Answer: There is little “regular” about PGA Tour players’ clubs. PGA Tour players are fitted by their club manufacturers to their specific wants and needs. The 4 iron you buy at Dicks will not necessarily look like the ones companies make for their players, and they’ll almost definitely not perform like the pro’s club. Many pros have the lofts and lies fully adjusted on their clubs. Ditto with drivers. Players will go to their club manufacturers and tinker for hours, maybe days until they get the driver trajectory and flight they want. They may make them slightly longer or slightly shorter depending on a dispersion chart. Standard retail length is around 45.5 inches. The Tour average is shorter actually, around 44.75 inches. Hitting fairways is a premium and all those guys hit the middle of the clubface more regularly with swings that create a ton of lag and speed, so they don’t always need that extra distance we crave in buying longer drivers. That said - we get those longer drivers and unfortunately because we don’t hit the center of the clubhead, we typically end up with errant shots.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why does clapping at golf sound different than in other sports?
Answer: Several reasons. The “golf clap” is sometimes a more polite clap than most. Not boisterous and rowdy, but appreciative. Microphone placement - where the mics are makes a difference in how the sound it picked up. Setting - golf is played outdoors in nature. When you hear applause at other events, it’s mixed in with cheers - sometimes you’ll get that same relative vibe at the closing holes of a golf tournament where thiings are often set up like an amphitheater around the 17th and 18th greens. Otherwise, you’re typically getting applause from one side of a green or fairway, one area, in a vast open space. Sound doesn’t reverberate in open space like it would in the confines of a stadium or arena.

Question: What is your opinion on former ESPN broadcaster Dan Patrick stating that steroids help you hit home runs?
Answer: Here’s where he’s right - more power may equal more homers. Popups becaome homers maybe because you’re stronger. Also, recovery from injury and advantages in extreme workloads (162 games in 180 days) is enhanced, so you may get back to hitting homers more quickly than those not on juice. Here’s where he’s absolutely wrong - Bonds’ hand/eye coordination was outstanding in Pittsburgh, before he ever started juicing. You can’t fake that with any juice. You have to have supreme hand/eye to hit the ball as consistently hard as Bonds did. Sad fact is he’d likely have challened Aaron’s record without the juice. Ditto with ARoid. These guys were all time greats before the junk because they were simply better at the game of baseball than even the most outstanding baseball players. And that’s because they saw it and hit it better than most ever before them or since them. Steroids might help you hit a homer when another guy is worn down at the 140th game in the season. Your extra strength may help you muscle out 2 homers a season. You may be injured and return sooner to hit another homer. But the reality is unless you see and hit the ball at the level of Bonds, you’re not getting big homers. How many other players juiced and weren’t remotely as successful? MANY. MOST. So I’m not 100% on Patrick’s statement. Yes, Bonds did wrong. Sullied the game. Absolutely some of his dingers were roided. But that fact that he hit the ball SO hard, SO often is a testament of his ability beyond the juice.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why is there such hostility towards Caitlin Clark in the WNBA?
Answer: Let’s say you’ve planted a seed. Your seed grows into a tree. That tree bears some small fruit. Not a huge yield, nothing major. Then a new farmer comes in and fertilizes that tree in ways you couldn’t. That tree now bears much more fruit. While you’re happy with the extra fruit, you’re a bit miffed that you couldn’t grow that fruit quite as well. That’s the Caitlin Clark story. I think most of the WNBA is somewhat annoyed, less with Clark and more with the overall situation. They’ve been playing great basketball and few have noticed. Then one person shows up and everything changes. Yeah, she’s the most prolific scorer in college basketball history. Case Keenum was the more prolific passer in college football history - he didn’t light the NFL on fire, nor did his appearance make the game more interesting. Sure there is a small amount of race issue there as well. It’s not lost on anyone that the fact that a person who is not black brought about all the attention, while the majority of the WNBA is black. There is some question as to how the marketing of humans in sport works. I think that’s a good part of the issue as well. I don’t think the WNBA dislikes Caitlin Clark as much as they dislike the system that creates the disparity. It’s very frustrating to have put out a good product before and the simple addition of one player makes it such that everything changes. Clark was a great college player. She didn’t walk into the WNBA and become the scoring leader immediately. She’s not the best player in the league. But she’s the attention getter. In time, the WNBA will show the fact that while there is disdain for the system that created this, they appreciate Clark because her presence will make them all a little richer. It will be similar to the Tiger Woods syndrome - you got tired of hearing about him, he was stirring the drink even when he wasn’t in contention - but he made the entire PGA Tour and all the players a ton more money they would have without him.

Question: Why does college football use a football with a white stripe while the NFL only uses a brown leather ball without the white stripes?
Answer: Today, it’s tradition and to separate college from the pros. In the past, it was necessity. While professional fields had better lighting, not all college stadiums had such great lighting. As well, many college stadiums had fields where the stands were only along the sidelines, with no seating in the end zones. It created something of a black hole for a football to come out of. The stripe on the college ball allowed it to be seen better coming from dark fields or darker zones on the field. Today, that’s not an issue - no stadium has such poor lighting. So it’s more a tradition that the college ball retains the half stripe near the ends.

Question: Are there any numbers of Covid infections reported from the maskless superbowl game?
Answer: Here’s what I found. It seems that 57 cases were linked to the 2021 Super Bowl. That would be 0.02% of the approximately 280,000 people that attended or were involved with the Super Bowl week activities. There may be more cases that weren’t reported or linked to the Super Bowl. But considering the number was so low based on what was actually reported, I think it would be a safe estimate that a ver small group was infected due to participation in that Super Bowl. And lets also remember, the SB wasn’t completely maskless - many celebrants did wear masks, which may have kept the number down. In the aftermath, the post game celebration, there were far more maskless people, but mostly outdoors. As long as social distancing was relatively good, the risk there was low. Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How did Oakland lose the Raiders, A’s, and Warriors?
Answer: How much time do you have? Short story: Billionaire owners looking for local municipalities to fund their stadiums, locals reap few of the benefits, when the city doesn’t want to help, owners shop their teams elsewhere because somewhere someone will pony up that dough. Oakland is a working-class town without the deep pockets to afford new stadiums. To suffice: it’s always about money. Adding on: The Warriors just went back home to San Francisco. Oracle Arena was built in 1966. It has hosted Johnny Cash, Sinatra, and Elvis. That’s an old building. Even with renovations, there is only so much to be done. New arenas spark new money. They make it easier to market to free agents who would be excited to play in a newer state of the art building. And Oakland was not going to pay to do more than renovate Oracle. That said, my guess is when the current owners bought the team, the idea was to move back to San Francisco unless Oakland was ready to build a new arena. As for the O.Co. that place is a dump. It’s a throw back to the multiuse stadiums of the 60’s and 70’s. You couldn’t attract solid free agents to Oakland to play there. They had been for years trying to get new stadia for the football and baseball teams in Oakland, but with Oakland being more a blue collar town, they weren’t interested in the tax repercussions of financing new builds. Las Vegas had been wanting a team for a long time and with football getting in bed with the gambling industry, the holdback from moving a team there waned. As for the A’s, it’s a similar situation. Theirs is compounded by poor ownership. The team has been a run so frugally, it was going to be hard to compete in a league with no salary cap. When you’re not competitive, no one comes to your games. When you play in a dump, no one comes to your games. When you’re not a winner, for certain no one will be willing to pony up tax dollars or bonds to help you build a new stadium. Again in short, other places offered upgraded solutions and Oakland wasn’t willing to play that game. It’s unfortunate for the fans, but billionaire owners are always looking for the next dollar without having to spend many dollars.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What if Tom Brady was drafted in the first round in the 2000 NFL draft? Would he have won a Super Bowl? Would the Patriots with Belichick have won a Super Bowl?
Answer: I’m not usually much for the “what if” fantasy questions. Not much to answer; it’s 100% speculative. In 2000 the Patriots didn’t even have a first round pick. That was part of the compensation for hiring Belichick from the Jets. So they couldn’t have used a first round pick on Brady. Were Brady drafted in the first round, he’d have been playing somewhere besides New England, at least to start his career. To further play into this fantasy, we’d have to assume that Brady’s college play was good enough to warrant a first round pick. It was not. He may not have been poor enough to say a 6th round pick - some may have rated him higher, but I don’t think any scout would have had him higher than an early 4th rounder. But playing along, you’d have to select which team you’d like Brady to have played for to note if he’d have been a Super Bowl winner. I’ve said this over and over - Brady alone didn’t win all those SB’s in New England. That top 10 defense had something to do with it also. So he’d have had to have gone to a team that was solid defensively and needed a QB. While I’m sure a lot of teams needed a QB, none of them were convinced Brady was the answer. As for the Patriots, I think if Drew Bledsoe returns from his injury and plays well, they are a playoff team. Would they have won a SB? No telling. Multiple SB’s? Who knows. Bledsoe was a prolific passer, and a Pro Bowl QB. I think he could have won there, if all the other factors remained constant - if Belichick had continued to work the team as he did, yeah, it was possible. Here’s where your fantasy should take shape… In the 2000 draft, there was only one QB taken in the first 2 rounds, Chad Pennington. Injuries derailed him from being better, but he was a good QB. So obviously no one was enamored with any QBs. In fact, the second QB chosen (and not selected until the 3rd round) was an absolute flyer - Giovanni Carmazzi of Hofstra (who don’t even play NCAA football anymore…). Here’s your fantasy - Carmazzi was drafted by the 49ers, the team Brady grew up idolizing. The Niners were a year removed from Steve Young by the 2000 draft. They were rolling with Jeff Garcia, a very serviceable QB, but not a Tom Brady. They hoped Carmazzi might be a diamond in the rough. The Niners played the Patriots in the annual Hall of Fame game in 2000. Yep, Brady faced Carmazzi. Carmazzi had an abysmal outing, completing 3 of 7 passes for 19 yards (Brady went 3 of 4 for 28 in less than 10 minutes of game time). There’s your storyline…. what if Brady gets taken by San Fran instead of Carmazzi? He gets to play for the team he cheered on from his northern California days. He walks in after Montana and Young and potentially continues the legend of Niner football. He plays for Steve Mariucci, who then may not get fired and maybe he gets the legacy of Walsh and Seifert. With Garcia in his 3rd and 4th seasons, they made the playoffs. Mooch’s teams were solid offensively. He inherited a good defensive team but they fell on hard times before rebounding to average. Maybe with Brady there they make better moves defensively. Maybe Brady there is Brady of New England. And maybe he’s as successful. But probably not…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: If I am throwing a foam ball 70 mph from 34 ft away from home plate to mound, how fast am I actually throwing considering the distance and the ball?
Answer: Ummm…. 70mph? What weighs more a ton of feathers or a ton of bricks? They weigh the same, a ton is a ton. You’d need zillions of feathers to make a ton, but it would still be a ton. If you’re throwing 70mph, the speed is still 70mph, regardless the type of ball or the distance. What you’re thinking and perceiving is what is the difference if you were throwing from 60ft 6in as the mound in baseball. But 70mph is 70mph. The difference is the distance, and - if there is a hitter - the reaction time because of distance. 70mph is a constant. The distance is the variable. As well, a foam ball may not have the same mass or weight of a baseball, so it may lose velocity more rapidly.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Are QB injuries in the NFL on the rise?
Answer: Yes. I think it’s a combination of things. The extra game is a small factor. Mobile QBs running the ball and getting hurt outside the pocket is also a factor. I think the biggest contributor is the emphasis on the passing game. Because there are more dropbacks now than ever, there are more opportunities for injuries to the QB. When the game was three yards and a cloud of dust, QB’s didn’t get hurt as much because they weren’t throwing as many passes. As dropbacks have increased, so have injuries. And it’s not just getting hit - several QB’s over the last few years have busted hands from hitting their hands on helmets as they passed the ball. The types of injuries run the gamut. Aaron Rodgers wasn’t hit when he popped his Achilles, but it was a pass play. Over the last 3 seasons, the number has increased exponentially. The additional game looks like cause and effect. I don’t know if that is fully accurate, but it certainly looks to be a factor. I’d like to see a couple of stats. While it would mirror the advent of the expansion of the passing game, I’d like to know how many injuries we saw when one more preseason game, more padded practices, and more live hitting in preseason. I’ve been saying this for years - the CBA that took away two-a-days and limited practice times and padded practices has softened the league. We see far too many injuries in the first month of the season because players aren’t adequately prepared to hit and be hit. And a number of the QB injuries fall into that category as well.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Can excessive practice hinder a golfer's chances of becoming a professional?
Answer: I think this is kind of a strange thought. The way a golfer becomes a professional is through excess amounts of practice. So in that sense, no, excessive practice does not hinder a golfer’s chance of becoming a pro. Beyond innate talent, excessive practice is the other key. That said, if the practice leads to paralysis by analysis - where you’re overdoing the examination of the swing, leaving yourself confused, or if you become injured or fatigued from overuse, then yeah, that can be an issue.

Question: Why is McIlroy ranked outside the top 50 on the PGA Tour in GIR percentage?
Answer: Why is Corey Connors in the top 10 on the PGA Tour in GIR percentage, and hasn’t missed a cut, yet only has two top 10 finishes in 17 events? Same type of question…. Only seven guys are above 70% and three of those guys don’t have 700 holes played. So Rory is fine where he is. I’m sure he’d like to be top 25% of the Tour, but it is what it is. And as yet, it’s not affecting his scoring. He’s got two wins this season and five top 10’s, he’s 3rd in the FedEx Cup race. He’s 3rd in total strokes gained. So the current 57th ranking in GIR isn’t hurting him. Plus there are 120 golfers below him who would gladly trade places with him.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is 16 too late to get into baseball with my only experience being from little league years ago? How should I go about learning different skills and practicing?
Answer: I’ll give a story of a player I coached. Guy comes out to try out for my American Legion team after he finished his senior year of high school, 17–18 years old. As it turns out I only had 17 players, and my limit was 18, so I could keep him. He had played football in high school, eschewing baseball since he was about 12 or 13. He was a left-handed pitcher, which made it more desirous to have him, as I had no other lefties. He struggled a lot, and he didn’t get to play much. He didn’t have command of his pitches and his delivery needed work. It was work that sadly was going to take more time than we had. We practiced for 2–3 weeks before hitting the regular season, playing 4–5 games a week for about 7–8 weeks. Because we had so many games, he did get to pitch some, mostly in non-district games and doubleheaders. But he was defininitely a fish out of water on the baseball field. Your situation is slightly different. If you’re trying to play high school ball, you’ll be afforded more time to work on skills, assuming you have the baseline talent to play. You’ve missed out on what I see as maybe 3 years of serious formative learning. That 13–15 window is when skills are really solidified for young players. Not saying you can’t do well or can’t catch up. It depends on your skill set and how well you adapt. But you are going to be at a competitive disadvantage. Your best practice would be to find a friend or a group of friends who play currently and work out with them. Ask them about the drills they do, find out what was required of them to make the team. The best way to practice is to do what they’re doing the way they do it. Ask them to help you. If there is a coach you can talk to, ask them what might be required and have them give you instructions on what they’d recommend you to do.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How in the world did the US Supreme Court decide that the US government does not have the right to ban bump stocks? Democrats, Republicans, Trump, the NRA, and more than 80% of all Americans supported banning bump stocks!
Answer: I don’t think the NRA’s “endorsement” of regulation of bump stocks was much more than an attempt to thwart further gun regulation. Kind of a thing where they say “we don’t want you messing with anything else, so we’ll give you this one”. It was a knee jerk reaction to the mass killing in Las Vegas in 2017. They knew they had little ground to stand on there. As for the Supreme Court decision, it’s only slightly quizzical, given the makeup of the court. But the scope of the question was narrow. The window they were looking through was small - does the bump stock in and of itself make a weapon automatic; meaning does the weapon itself change characteristics. And the answer to that is no. The bump stock is an individual object. It cannot on its own be considered automatic weaponry, despite it’s singular use. The bump stock uses a semi automatic weapon’s recoil to allow the gun to fired in rapid succession. What it doesn’t do is allow a single pull of the trigger to fire off multiple shots - the recoil of the bump stock bounces the weapon allowing multiple pulls in rapid succession. Yep, that’s it - the question that was asked of the Supreme Court was probably the wrong one, and they gave the only possible answer. I’d also be willing to bet the question posed to the Court was set up that way by the NRA. They would not want to make the bump stock manufacturers upset, and they knew how to work around their own words. So the decision of the SC, despite it’s ridiculousness, was the correct answer given the question asked and our definition of automatic weapons. The government can ban automatic weapons, but it can’t ban a device used to make a weapon automatic unless the specific function of that device is to make multiple shots fire rapidly with one pull of the trigger. It doesn’t matter that the reality is you only depress your finger one time and the bump stock does the rest, apparently.

Question: How do professional golfers earn money if they don't win tournaments but make cuts during them?
Answer: Each tournament has a prize purse. That is all the monies available to the players who make the cut. You play Thursday and Friday, basically for free. If you don’t make the cut, you don’t get paid for the week (the US Open paid every participant who didn’t make the cut $10k, except for the amateurs who couldn’t receive that money). If you make the cut, you get a percentage of the purse, dependent on your finish. The winner in the regular events gets 18% of the total purse. Second place gets 10%. It goes on down to the last place, which gets 0.215% of the prize money. The breakdown is different for majors I think.

Question: How do you think the increasing prize money in golf championships like the U.S. Open affects the competitiveness and motivation of professional golfers?
Answer: To be honest, the prize money in the majors isn’t the biggest motivation. Winning a major championship is it’s own motivation. There are only four majors per season, and the fields contain the best players on the planet. Winning a major means golf immortality. Your name goes alongside the greatest players ever to play the game. It’s the one time guys like Ben Curtis, Shaun Micheel, Rich Beem, and Michael Campbell get some love. Their name is on plaques and trophies alonside the greatest players in the game. So the money is less relevant for the majors. The money is nice, but your name on a trophy with Jack, Ben, and Tiger is WAY more important.

Question: Can someone become a full-time professional golfer if they are dedicated and passionate about the game, but not skilled enough to play on tour?
Answer: Sure. You can go to school to learn to be a Professional Golfers of America pro and you can learn to teach the game to others. If you are a PGA professional, you are considered a professional golfer because you teach the game. Tour golfers play the game for pay, PGA pros teach the game for pay. To earn the right to be a PGA professional, there is a competence playing exam, but you don’t have to shoot par to pass the exam. I think you have to be able to shoot the course rating plus 15 strokes for 2 rounds. So if you’re playing a par 72 course and the rating is 72, then you’d have to shoot a total of 159 or less over 2 rounds. That gives you some leeway. Not many people are skilled enough to play on tour - that’s a unique talent. But there are tens of thousands of dedicated and passionate golfers who enjoy the game and love to share it though education.

Question: Why do professional golfers take so long to play a round of golf?
Answer: Because everything counts. One of the reasons it doesn’t take an amateur longer to play is often because amateurs don’t play by every rule. Also, when amateurs miss a shot, there is little repurcussion. When a professional misses a shot, there are tens of thousands of dollars on the line. Sometimes those things are the difference between winning and losing. We eyeball putts and roll them. They methodically examine putts in a way that amateurs don’t. Not saying all this is necessary. Many times they take too long and still miss. That’s why I watch and appreciate guys like the rookie Åberg who puts the club behind the ball and swings, or Tony Finau who puts his putter behind the ball and just goes. But the real reason is because every stroke counts and you’d never want to give away a stroke on something silly like rushing a stroke.

Question: What happens at a PGA Tour Championship golf course after the tournament?
Answer: Sometimes the Quora bot question creator thingy is a bit wonky. Is is a PGA Tour course, a PGA Championship course, or the Tour Championship course? So any PGA Tour course will have a ton of let down work to do after the tournament. Immediately after the tournament ends, the TV and Tour crews start removing hundreds of miles of wires that have laid out around the course. In the days after, there will be crews taking down all the stands that were erected, all the tents for concessions and souvenirs. As for the course itself, tour courses are set to a certain standard. It’s a standard the course won’t be at any other time of the year. It’s not easy to get the grass on the greens cut so low and tight on the daily. But for the tour, they make the exception because the course has to test the best players in the world. It’s why sometimes you see the greens turning yellow or brownish by the weekend of tournaments - they shave those greens down. Typically, though, there’s not much to be done with the course itself. They’ll cut the grasses more to the norm, less rough, slightly higher with the blades on the green. Maybe they cut the fairways a bit wider, ease up some angles on doglegs.

Question: Can you scrap old golf clubs?
Answer: Best is to sell them. Clubs inside of 30 years old will typically have some small value; may not be much, but if you’re selling bulk, you can make a few bucks. Very old clubs will have no value, unless they’ve been kept pristine for years and maybe can sell as antiques. If you have an old persimmon that’s hardly used with the ferrule still in good shape and no marks or scarring, someone may want that. Or you can take them and use them in your garden to tie up your tomato plants and other wandering garden growth…

Question: Do you think Tiger Woods will be able to make a comeback in future golf tournaments despite his recent struggles?
Answer: No, not only are Tiger’s best days behind him, winning at all is going to be a challenge. Here’s the thing. Tiger had a mental Rolodex of shots. If he needed a 163 yard shot that went high, landed soft, bounced once and checked up, he could pull that shot out regularly and hit it. If he needed a low 2-iron stinger that traveled 257 yards, he could do that on command. When there was a putt he absolutely had to make, he made it. He can no longer just hit all those shots on command. He can still hit them, but not on command in a tournament round. Because he can only play so few rounds of competitive golf, and because he can’t practice like he used to, those shots are lost. He can still play golf. He’s still one of the better golfers in the world. But as we watched in the US Open this week, Tiger just couldn’t command all those shots. Yes, the course was tough and we saw even Scottie Scheffler, the world’s best golfer today, struggle to make the cut. But golfers made the cut and hit some of the shots they needed on command. Leader Åberg hit the shots Tiger and Jack used to hit - those high irons that landed like butterflies with sunburned feet. And he typically placed them on the green in just the spots they needed to be. Tiger doesn’t get to rehearse those enough anymore to have great command over them. And he doesn’t play enough competitive rounds to be in competitive round form. What we’re seeing from Tiger now is what we’ll consistently see from him as he winds down his competitive career on the regular PGA Tour. Is it possible for him to catch lightning in a bottle and play well enough for 4 days to compete? Hard to say. I can see him making a cut if he were in a regular event playing in warm weather with few hills. This tournament set up well for him in that sense, but the greens are treacherous and unless you’re on your game, you’re going to miss shots and have tough recoveries. And if Tiger is playing and practicing less, we know he’s not going to spend as much time on the tough recoveries. That puts him at a competitive disadvantage. And as he gets older, while he can still hit it a long way and still has the ability to hit all the shots, that command gets harder and harder because of age. What age takes away it doesn’t give back.

Question: How do you think the negotiations between Alvin Kamara and the New Orleans Saints will unfold in the coming months?
Answer: Tough situation. Kamara comes into this season as the second highest paid RB in the NFL, so not too shabby. But his contract is up in 2025, and there is no guaranteed money in 2025. Plus, Kamara will count $29 million towards the Saints’ cap next season. No guarantee, and that cap hit make Kamara almost certainly a cap casualty in 2025. Cutting him would only hit the Saints for $10 million; that hit is easier than paying him what they owe him next year. So Kamara isn’t into this for more money, he just wants to play for the Saints for the rest of his career. And don’t get it twisted - that’s not his “love” for the Saints as much as it is the fact that this season Kamara will play at 29 years old. We all already know the 30 year old RB doesn’t get paid. If Kamara were to be released after this season, he’d not command much on the open market. His biggest and best value is to the team that already knows him, the Saints. If another team were to want him, he could maybe force the Saints to pay him or trade him. But I don’t know that he has a ton of suitors. He is under contract this season, so the Saints are under no obligation to deal with any of this until this season is over. Kamara’s only leverage is to hold out and try to force the Saints to make something happen now. But the Saints may simply move forward. The leverage is relatively even. Kamara can play hardball and force the Saints to make a move. And the Saints likely will because this offense won’t work without Kamara or someone like him. That said, the Saints are under no obligation to pay Kamara - he’s under contract. They can roll through the season and hope he plays up to his standard, and then be faced with the same situation next season. I could be the Saints’ tack - especially since re-signing him when he’s turning 30 could be easier on their wallet. I honestly don’t know what the Saints will do. They aren’t a team that leaves clear tracks on handling situations like this. And to be honest, they don’t end up in this situation often - particularly not with a player walking out of camp. One thing the Saints pride themselves on is handling situations like this quietly behind closed doors. Kamara has made a statement of this. It would surprise me if this isn’t resolved by early training camp, before August. I don’t think the Saints want to bring it into camp and have it linger into time for Kamara to get into this offense.

Question: How long to walk through the National WWII Museum in New Orleans, minus Beyond all Boundaries, Freedom Theater and the Submarine experience? I plan to dedicate about 2 1/2 hours to the museum outside of these exhibits.

Question: How crucial is it for young defensive players like Payton Turner and Isaiah Foskey to step up in light of injuries to key pass rushers on the New Orleans Saints roster?

In fact, the Saints would pull Jordan often on rushing downs to get more speed off the edges. So it’s up to Turner, Foskey, Granderson, and newly acquired Chase Young to provide that giddy-up. And to stay healthy. Those guys, if healthy, could be very formidable. Turner is the complete package. At 6′6″, 270, he’s a behemoth. He has the physical standing of a Myles Garrett (Turner is actually taller) and could be a disruptive force. So far though, the only thing he’s disrupted in the rehab schedule…

Question: How was Peyton Manning able to complete so many passes while his throwing skills were the minimum level required to play quarterback?

Question: Is there a catch-all clause in any NFL contract that would prohibit a football player from taking a knee during the national anthem?
Answer: First, a question back - why? It does nothing to affect the actual playing of the football game. Protest is LITERALLY the action that created this country; disallowing that freedom would be more un-American than the kneeling itself. Now, to answer the question, there is no clause that you could put in a contract that would accomplish that. Any clause would be unconstitutional, and no league would want the government/Supreme Court interfering with the league. But… players don’t play for the NFL, they play for teams. The NFL adjudicates the league, but the team owners write the players’ checks and create team guidelines. So, could a team put it in their contract? Again, no - unconstitutional. Could they create a team rule that says you can’t kneel? Sure they could. And the player would be breaking the rule in kneeling, which could lead to a fine, suspension, or release. However…I would NOT want to be the owner that decides to die on that hill though. Say Mahomes decides he wants to kneel but the Hunts tell him not to. He does it anyway. Well, they can’t not pay him - they both signed a contract. They could fine him - but he makes $45 million a year, so…. big whoop, and an ENORMOUS distraction/PR nightmare. They’re left with a suspension or dismissal. Yeah, that’s not happening. But what WOULD later happen if they went that route is Mahomes would demand a trade and would eventually get one, and then you’re the Chiefs of the 1980s. So, good luck with that. Here’s another thought - should each stadium create a fan code of conduct that says people must stop where they are, remove their hats, and place their hands over their hearts when the anthem is played? No sales of beer or hot dogs, no selling a jersey or taking tickets, no moving in the venue, no talking? Because that’s more disrespectful than kneeling - at least kneeling is deferential and you’re not moving.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What factors does the PGA tour consider when selecting golf courses for tournaments?
Answer: Most courses on Tour have been on the Tour’s schedule for years. But when a new one is considered, they look at a number of factors. Obviously first and foremost is whether or not the course layout itself is worthy of a PGA Tour event - does it have enough strength to challenge the world’s best golfers? Will it be a sufficient test of the golfers? They work away from that - who is the designer and what are their bona fides? What courses have they designed before? Does the course have some history or legacy? Tour courses usually fall into a couple of categories - private courses or resort courses (or Tournament Players Courses - TPC). The Tour will have to be able to have some say so in how the course prepares for a tournament. Often the private courses love to host a tournament because it enhances the prestige of the course. As well the tour and/or sponsors will partner with a worthy course to do capital improvements for their tournament. Then there’s infrastructure. Is the course near a city or in a remote location? If remote, how remote? What is the nearby big city; does it have other attractions? How easy is it to get fans to the course and back? How efficient is transportation? Where/how is parking? Will there be places to bring in Tour related semi-trailers? Will there be space for concessions and setting up stands? Is there a willing local sponsor to put it on? And of course, the title sponsor may want to have a say so in the course selection.

Question: What is a deep post route in football?

Question: What led to the change in dominance from "The Big Three" (Tiger Woods, Phil Mickelson, Ernie Els) to the current state of the PGA Tour?
Answer: Hmm…. Big Three? I’d posit it was more the big ONE and a few satellites. And if were going to call it a group, we might do well to include Vijay Singh and Retief Goosen. Tiger was number one for most of the 2000’s first decade, spending only 32 weeks outside the number one spot (Vijay had each of those 32 weeks). But the years since Tigers last run (almost a year from 2013 to 2014) have seen a more volatile mix of number ones and a good bit more movement at the top. More guys have jockeyed for position at the top. The depth of field is what has been different. Today’s fields are stronger top to bottom. There are still a few guys around the top that could be today’s “Big #” candidates. Obviously Scheffler is at the top of the heap, but you could include guys like Schauffele, Morikawa, and McIlroy to that list. While Scheffler is on something of a historic run, we have to wait to see if it is a “Tiger-esque” run. But currently, Scheffler is dominating in a fashion we haven’t seen since Tiger’s ascension. But to more accurately answer the question the change is due to time. Els and Mickelson, along with Vijay and Goosen are all over 50 now. Tiger will turn 50 in 2025. So time passed them (not to mention Tiger’s injuries taking him out of the game before his dominance was done). And the current state isn’t much different from any other state, save for the fact that many of the great golfers don’t play on the PGA Tour anymore through their own choice.

Question: What do you think about Nick Piazza's injury working on the New Orleans Saints chain crew? Are sideline skirmishes a common occurrence?

This particular incident was something that didn’t look like it was going to end up off the field. Kamara’s incredible balance is what took it off the field. Piazza had to have some surgery to get his leg put back together. He allegedly plans on returning to the sidelines.

Question: Why were there no teams interested in signing Drew Brees before he joined the New Orleans Saints?
Answer: Well, actually there was a team very interested. The Miami Dolphins brought Brees in and Nick Saban truly wanted to sign him. But the medical staff intervened and warned him off due to the nature of Brees’ injury. Which brings us to why no other teams were interested - the injury. Brees had been a decent but not stellar QB in San Diego. When the opportunity to draft a QB came up, San Diego went and got Eli Manning (who they knew wouldn’t play for them) and then worked out the trade for Philip Rivers. Rivers was their future QB. Brees retained the job for a season while Rivers learned and held Rivers’ ascencion to starter off for a year as the Chargers made the playoffs behind him in 2004. But at the end of the 2005 season, Brees was injured badly in a game and his entire NFL future was questionable. And now, they had their future QB in Rivers anyway, so Brees was expendable. Because of the type of injury it was, the prognosis wasn’t clear nor positive for Brees to return to form so everyone passed on him. Including Miami at the 11th hour. So he basically fell into the Saints’ lap. Saints won that deal. Rivers led the Chargers to the playoffs 6 times in his 14 years as the starter there, and only one AFC Championship. Saban only coached 2 seasons, Daunte Culpepper never regained his form after his injury. Gus Frerotte and Joey Harrington ended up as the more prominent Dolphins QB’s in Saban’s seasons. And the Dolphins went to the playoffs twice in the time that Brees played for the Saints. Meanwhile, the Saints went to the NFC Championship in Brees’ first season in New Orleans, and returned to that championship 3 seasons later and won a Super Bowl. In Brees 15 seasons as the starter, the Saints were in the playoffs 9 times and went to 3 NFC Championships. Brees will be a first ballot HOFer and is considered one of the all-time greats, having retired with the most passing yards in NFL history.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do you think Bill Belichick always believed that he could make the Cam Newton situation work?
Answer: I think Belichick saw the rest of the league and took a shot at going far in a different direction than he was used to. I don’t think the goal was to turn Newton into Brady, but to have a QB who could extend plays with his legs and get some first downs on the ground. Belichick also knew his defense could keep them in games, he just needed competent play at QB to make them viable. Despite his flaws, Newton did have upside - size, mobility, and experience. I think Bill saw those things - and that the rest of the NFL was looking at mobile QBs - and made a business decision. I don’t think he takes him if he didn’t at least believe he could work out.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What caused the Oakland Raiders (now Las Vegas Raiders) to have losing seasons from 2003-2015?
Answer: The story is similar to the Cowboys futility since 1995…. The Raiders drafted poorly, made poor personnel moves, picked the wrong coaches, had some less than stellar front office personnel… basically doing all the wrong things. Over that 13 year span they had 9 different people who head coached games for them, including interim guys. Not good. They had one decent QB in Carr in that period. In that time frame, RBs were still a thing, but they only had four 1000 yard rushing seasons. In three seasons, their top receiver was a TE. Anything that could go wrong did, until they got competent at head coach. Del Rio righted the ship and got them moving in the right direction. But even then, they fired him after 3 seasons and gave the whole franchise to Gruden.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Will Bo Nix have the same success as Drew Brees under Sean Payton?
Answer: The Brees/Payton team in New Orleans was a match made in heaven, a dream scenario. A new fresh faced coach comes to a team whose city had just faced the worst natural disaster in recorded American history. The team was coming off a 3–13 season. Brees had been released by San Diego after a major injury put his career in jeopardy. Even Miami was scared to touch him becuase it was too much a risk. They came in with zero expectations and zero pressure. It was easy to create under those circumstances. Brees’ arm came back gradually and the Saints went on to greatness, and Brees is now a first ballot shoo-in HOF player, one of the legends of the game. Payton will not have the same success with any other QB, not likely ever or anywhere. Brees is one of the best to ever play - not many will ever achieve that. Payton is already under a much different set of circumstances there. He’s not taking over a completely devastated program. There are already expectations. And Nix is not even remotely close to Brees in ability.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is training in American football ultimately a subpar investment of time for most young boys given the propensity of injuries (e.g. concussions), that few will make the NFL, & even most that do will be low-draft picks with little guaranteed money?
Answer: IF you are training to become a professional football player, then yes, it’s a subpar investment because the odds are stacked largely against you. If you are training because you want to be part of a team, because you want to make lifelong friends and have stories to share forever, because you want to be a productive part of that team and pull your own weight, then you’re on the perfect path and it’s an outstanding investment of your time.

Question: After a Chiefs player had a cardiac arrest at their practice today, do you think it is time for the NFL to quit starting the season so early while it is still very hot? How about starting in November and extend it into March or April?
Answer: This isn’t the answer to the question, but the player in question was in a team meeting, not in the middle of a practice. So unless they’d just come in from outdoor work, heated practice wouldn’t seem the issue for a collapse or cardiac arrest. My guess is once they run tests, they will find some heart related issue that led to the situation. I think the NFL is not interested in running their season completely and directly over basketball. If the NBA wanted to move their season to run during the summer, maybe - but then you have the domino effect of having to also move the WNBA season… I do not think the NFL is concerned with moving the season. There are really only 4 teams that truly have real heat concerns. And every team has an indoor facility to work in when the temperatures are extreme.

Question: Which new pairing of coach and quarterback in the NFL for the 2024 season are you most excited to see?
Answer: There are a few intriguing combinations to look at, but I’m sure the one most people are interested in is Jim Harbaugh with Justin Herbert. Herbert has slowly developed and is already thought of as one of the more purely talented QB’s in the league. But to really make a mark, he needs to consistently make the playoffs. Name: Tony Twillie
Question: As a golf enthusiast, what advice would you give to Miles Russell as he prepares for his debut on the PGA Tour?
Answer: Enjoy the moment. Don’t get so caught up in trying to make the cut or impress the pros there or the fans that you don’t enjoy the moment. You’re getting the opportunity of a lifetime - one you may never get again. There is no guarantee you’ll be a PGA Tour golfer, nor that you’ll even want to be in 6 or so years. Smile. Laugh. Look at people and embrace the moment. Don’t get me wrong - that doesn’t mean don’t grind over shots. That doesn’t mean don’t practice. That doesn’t mean don’t work hard and try hard. Those things aren’t mutually exclusive. You can work hard while you’re there AND enjoy the moment. And that’s what he should strive for. And when that moment comes to an end, thank the people who made it possible and be humble.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do professional golfers carry all of their clubs during every round, or do they only use certain sets for specific situations such as short game or long game?
Answer: Pro golfers will almost always carry all 14 clubs during a stipulated tournament round. There is no advantage to carrying fewer clubs. What they may do, depending on the course and conditions, is swap certain clubs in and out of the bag. For example if you play at Augusta National, their sand is different from the sand you’d encounter at any Open Championship course. So you may swap your sand wedge for Augusta - which would maybe have a lot of bounce - for one with less bounce playing at St. Andrews. Or if you play a course with consistently tight lies, again, you may opt for your sand wedge with less bounce over one with a lot of bounce where the club might bounce off the turf. Or if you don’t feel you’re going to need to hit a 5-wood or 3-iron maybe you carry an extra wedge. Those are things you may look at as you play a practice round at the course.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How many NFL players are not millionaires?
Answer: Lots of them. The league minimum salary is $795k per season. There will be many players who play for this salary and won’t play more than a season or two. Even if you make that much in two seasons (though your second season will likely come with an increase), you will have made “only” a bit less than $1.6 million. Factor taxes and expenses in and you still haven’t really topped $1 million. And remember, when we say millionaire, that’s net worth, not just salary. Once we factor in liabilities, that million gets even smaller. Yeah, you bought that $125,000 car, but you’re making payments - that is a liability. And as time goes on, that asset depreciates in value, so you don’t have a $125k car - it’s worth less than that. The number of players who play 2–4 years in the league outnumbers the players who stay long term, so you don’t have as many millionaires as you’d imagine. Most players aren’t comfortably millionaires unless they are top 5 round picks who stay for a few years, or until they get their second contract. And the rookie salary minimum won’t hit $1 million until 2029. So until that season, no one will actually be an “instant millionaire”.

Question: Does the College Football Hall of Fame induct more players than the Pro Football Hall of Fame?

Considering the number of players, the college HOF has a far smaller percentage of players in.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: It does seem to be the case that blacks are naturally dominant in sporting activities that demand physique, mental fortitude and stamina. Examples are athletics, boxing and basketball. What accounts for this phenomenon?
Answer: I think since there have been less than 80 black NHL players throughout history, that those who play hockey would like a word with you on blacks dominating sports requiring physique, mental fortitude, and stamina… Athletic dominance is created by a complex melange of factors; not the least of which is a ton of practice. There are certain traits of a population that may assist in athletic endeavors - people from certain areas of the world may have genetically inherited traits that allow for certain abilities to be more easily gained. Others have socio-economic factors that may lead to a perspective in which working harder at a sport could provide advantages for a person. In addition with the socio-economic factors, being able to afford to play certain sports is a factor. Environmental factors play a role as well - Scandinavians are tremendous at outdoor winter sports - is it because they’re white? No one would say that. It’s because of where they live. As well, if we talk about genetic predisposition, then shouldn’t it logically follow that Irish people make great police officers, or Jewish people are logically going to be the best comedians since there are historically an abundance of both groups in those professions? We don’t think of those things that way, so why would we think of sports as such? It shows the fact that there are a lot of reasons things happen the way they do that ae beyond race (which is a social construct anyway…).

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How difficult is the transition from alloy bats to wooden bats when a college baseball player enters the professional level?

It takes some time to adjust to the feel, the way the ball comes off the bat, the smaller sweet spot. The biggest transition is to dealing with better pitching regularly.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why when I try to get in a catchers stance, I fall backwards? I always hear people say put your feet flat on the ground and stop being on your toes, but when I try and put my feet flat I just fall back instantly, someone please help
Answer: There is no such thing as squatting flat footed. Yes, you will fall because your body will be out of balance. And if you don’t fall, the position you’re in leaves you in no position to be able to catch a pitched ball. The catcher’s stance is always on the balls of your feet. You are squatted, square to the pitcher on the balls and toes of your feet. Unless you’re adopting the new “stance” that catchers are using, the kickstand where they’re actually on a knee and low to the ground. Good luck blocking pitches anywhere but directly in front of you in that position… Good catcher stances are easily researchable with YouTube videos.

Question: How did people buy NBA or NFL tickets before the internet? Could you call up ticketmaster on your cord phone at home give them a credit card number and they'd mail you tickets through fedex or ups, or right to your mail box?
Answer: As I age, I enjoy questions like this - and of course cringe at my age and knowledge of things of this nature. I remember going to wait in lines for tickets to so many things pre-internet. Concert tickets came out and there would be lines forever at Ticketmaster outlets…. Typically, yes, you could call and purchase tickets, or you could go to the arena box office and purchase them. Tickets came either in the mail or shipped via courier service. Or you could go to Will Call and pick them up. Tickets were physical up until a few years ago - you had a physical ticket that you showed at the door or gate. Recently with that, there was a scanner that scanned the ticket, before that, the ticket had a stub which was ripped off as you entered. Crazy times, those 1900s…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How is average viewership for NFL games calculated? Do they include estimates for piracy? Is it just people who watch on cable, parties or families watching together, etc.?
Answer: Nielsen designates a sample size of households and individuals to be their raters. The estimate for viewership is extrapolated from that number, as a percentage of viewership. There are also devices today that Nielsen designated people can wear and take with them, so if you’re at a bar watching or at a home that is not your own, it would note that you’re not home (GPS) and also pick up what you’re watching away from home. Yes, it’s Orwellian, but in this case, you have to agree to be a Nielsen household, so you know you’re being tracked. Piracy wouldn’t really matter for average viewership numbers - even a pirated signal would be counted as viewing. That’s really more a FCC thing; noting that people aren’t paying for their services. The one thing they are working at getting better at is determining who is streaming and not, because that’s a newer development. Not all people watch broadcast anymore, so determining how people are watching, and on what devices, is the next layer of this. It’s far from perfect, but it’s the best we can do.

Question: Which tight end is better: the one who is great at blocking but not as good at receiving, or the one who is great at receiving but not as good at blocking?

If you’re looking for a more in-line TE, you’re looking more at a guys like a Dalton Schulz or a Dawson Knox. They’re going to catch passes, but you’re looking for them to be very adept in blocking as well. Then, you have the unicorn. George Kittle is an outstanding blocker and an outstanding pass catcher. If you could have anyone, you’d want him. And maybe Mark Andrews. In most of today’s offenses with a strong passing attack, you’ll sacrifice a small amount of blocking for a guy who can catch 50–60 passes a season and get you 5–8 TDs.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: In the MLB, is there ever a situation where the batter could/would realistically attempt to steal first base?
Answer: No. There isn’t any way to achieve first base other than the ones that are already in the rule book - hit, fielding error, fielder’s choice, hit by pitch, walk, intentional walk, interference. The last instance would be the dropped third strike, but that doesn’t count as a steal. That is ruled a strikeout, and then either a passed ball or a wild pitch.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why isn’t Troy Aikman considered the greatest 90s quarterback despite winning 3 super bowls?
