It’s great to win Super Bowls. But those wins don’t necessarily mean you were the best QB of your day. Aikman was never an All-Pro. He made the Pro Bowl a bunch, but that only means he was a top 3–5 QB (or that better QB’s didn’t want to play…). Only once did he throw for more than 20 TDs, and he has 141 interceptions to his 165 TDs; not outstanding. Only once was he in consideration for the league MVP, and even that was only a 5th place finish for him. For his career, the people whose careers his most resembled were guys like Jim Kelly, Kenny Stabler, and Terry Bradshaw. All very nice QBs, all Hall of Famers, but none the best of their day. I’d have Kelly in front of Aikman for better in the 1990s, not to mention Steve Young, Brett Favre, and without question John Elway.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do I keep improving my basketball no matter my age? I feel I am unlimited, but why do some NBA players even seem to have a limit in their skills, not no limit?
Answer: Because once you reach a certain level of proficiency, improvement is modest, almost imperceptible. You feel unlimited because you are likely young and growing into who you will become. You have so much more to learn and even as your body develops, more changes in your game occur. Conrast that with an NBA player who is 30 years old. They have already developed the skills you’re working on. Their improvement comes less with being able to jump higher, move quicker, shoot better. Their improvement comes in recognizing a screen and being able to rub off it more efficiently. Or seeing a cut coming and moving into a passing lane. Or being a split second quicker with your hands to deflect a pass because you’ve seen this pass a hundred times. Or being able to move to a better spot for a set up jumper. Those aren’t the improvements of a teenager, or even an early 20-something. Those are the improvements of a veteran player who has seen things. And here’s the negative. Around the time you’re mastering all the nuances that improve your game, you lose a step in speed and agility because you’re getting older. That’s why for professional athletes, there a very small window of greatness; that time with athletic ability, maturity, and knowledge are all maximized. Only the incredibly great ones hold that window open longer.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why isn’t Terry Bradshaw considered the greatest 70s quarterback despite winning 4 super bowls?

But there aren’t many others who anyone would consider “better”. Bert Jones may have had the most passing talent of all of them, but his team wasn’t great. That’s the other factor for Bradshaw - his defense was outstanding, so that takes a little of the spotlight. And if we just look at individual numbers, not just wins and championships, Bradshaw only completed 52% of his passes and has 2 more TDs than interceptions for his career. Those aren’t earth shaking numbers. Despite playing with pretty good receivers, didn’t even hit 30k yards passing in his career. He’s still considered a great of his era because he was better in the playoffs and won 4 rings.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why are the Oakland/Los Angeles Raiders, who won three Super Bowls from 1976 to 1983, not considered a dynasty?

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Founded in 1988, which team is the original Charlotte Hornets now, the Pelicans or the Hornets?
Answer: The Hornets reclaimed their history in the 2014–2015 season. When the Hornets moved to New Orleans in 2002, the NBA orchestrated a deal to return a franchise to Charlotte. When the Bobcats formed, they were formed as an expansion team in the league. At that time, all the Hornets team records were in New Orleans. In 2014, the New Orleans team changed their name to the Pelicans and the Hornets retook their name. As part of the deal, the Pelicans were treated as a pseudo-expansion team. The Hornets were restored all their team records up to 2002, and then they merged those records with the Bobcats records, and now they are Hornets/Bobcats/Hornets records. However, the Pelicans retain those records for the Hornets from their time in New Orleans, so everything that happened in New Orleans stays in New Orleans, but what happened before New Orleans in 2002 goes back to Charlotte. While I like the Pelicans name well enough, can we please get the Jazz to give up a name that has never - ever - fit them in Utah?

Question: What do you think the potential impact of Ken Dorsey, the Browns' new offensive coordinator, will be on Deshaun Watson's performance this season?

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why did the NFL Chicago Cardinals leave Chicago at the start of the 1960 season? My father was born in 1947, and he told me that there were a lot of Cardinals fans in Chicago and they were popular.
Answer: Popular, maybe, but not good. The Cardinals won 33 games in the 1950s….. total, for the entire decade. They weren’t good and attendance stunk. They became the FAR second fiddle to the Bears and as such they looked to leave town. They were fortunate in that the AFL started play in 1960…. The Bidwells were trying to find a place to play outside of Chicago, but they weren’t willing to relinquish control of the team, plus the NFL was asking a lot for relocation fees. The AFL coming online was an issue for the NFL, so they fast tracked the Cardinals’ move to St. Louis to make sure an AFL team couldn’t be placed there.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Are you surprised that Travis Kelce and Patrick Mahomes defended Harrison Butker during his controversy?
Answer: Not at all. If you have a job in a place with more than 2 employees, it’s almost guaranteed that you will not agree on everything. It is a guarantee that every NFL player is not the same. They come from different places and different backgrounds. They will have varying opinions on a lot of things. But at the NFL level, they have all done similar hard work to get there, and continue to do hard work to stay there. That earns you the respect of your co-workers. You don’t have to love them. You don’t even have to like them. You may simply respect the work they do and move along. Players often move in different circles and may not have much interaction at all with some other players. It’s fine because they’re all there for one goal - to win football games. You don’t have to invite them over for dinner, or go to the movies, or play cards with them. That’s not the way of the world. Can you imagine 45 year old Tom Brady trying to buddy up with a 21 year old teammate? Doesn’t even make logical sense. Such is the case with Butker. The players understand that this is his opinion, they don’t have to share it. They simply are on the same team. They will support him as a teammate on the field and defend his right to speak his mind.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do you believe Aaron Rodgers' public endorsement of Nathaniel Hackett will alleviate pressure on the Jets coaching staff?
Answer: No. First, Rodgers is a kook, so what he says doesn’t hold a ton of weight. Second, the Jets have sucked for a long time now. Hackett’s only claim is that he lets Rodgers do what he wants.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What is the highest paying sport for athletes, excluding endorsements, and why? Is there a significant difference in pay between the NBA, MLB, NFL, NHL, and PGA Tour golfers?
Answer: If we’re talking averages, the NBA has the highest average salaries, at $10.82 (just behind Formula One racers). Baseball follows but far behind at around $5 million. Hockey is next at $3.5 million and surprisingly to many, the NFL would bring up the rear in average salary at $2.8 million a year. So yes, there is a significant difference between the average NBA player, and the average NFL player. Why? Well, despite the NFL dwarfing the total revenue of the NBA (and every other major sport on earth), there are far more people to pay in the NFL. NFL rosters are 53 players, as well as a host of coaches and support personnel. The NBA roster is only 15 players with fewer support personnel. MLB has a 26 man roster, and the NHL 23. As for the PGA Tour, it’s not as much a “league” as a collection of individual contractors under one umbrella. It functions far different from the other major sports - you don’t have to play every week, your pay is based completely on production, you only get paid the top money if you win. It’s got more in common with auto racing than the big 4–5 sports where they play in leagues. The PGA Tour average for 2023 was $2.36 million a year. That’s only earnings. And while that’s an average, that is good enough for 81st place on the money list. Sounds really great considering 241 golfers made at least one paycheck last season. And it sounds like the average is skewed towards the top of the list. But that finish would have left you out of the season ending money in the FedEx Cup race. However, you would be in the Top 125 and retain your card for another season.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What are some possible explanations for why so many NFL players have a low net worth despite making millions of dollars?
Answer: The definition and calculation of net worth is assets minus liabilities. Many pro athletes have lots of liabilities but few assets. First, let’s back up. The average NFL salary is just under $3 million, but we’ll say $3m for the sake of discussion. You’re in the top tax bracket so by the time all is done, you’re taking home just over $1.5 million. Now, that is OUTSTANDING money. But it’s not life altering money. If you’re 24 years old, you’re not going to live the rest of your life on $1.5 million dollars. And the NFL is not for long, so if you only make that money for 3 seasons, you’re not wealthy. You’re “rich”, and you can parlay that money into a lot more money, but you’re not wealthy enough to have and maintain a high net worth. Now, let’s say you’re a younger player in the league. You’re going to have cash, and you’re likely to put some money in savings. As for a car, that’s a nice today asset, but cars depreciate, so unless you bought an antique car, it’s not holding value for your net worth. You’re not likely out with your early earnings buying real estate. You may buy a home, but you’re going to have a mortgage likely, which is a liability, taking away from your net worth. Unless you paid cash for that car, you have an auto loan. You are lucky that you likely got a full scholarship so you don’t have any student loan debt. But often players take out personal loans early because they don’t have cash on hand, and that consumer debt is a liability. This is why players often have low net worths. They borrow against their future earnings so they have money, but not assets, and their liabilities take away from their net worth.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do you think the Green Bay Packers are "nothing to play with"?
Answer: I think if you are a Packers fan, you have to be delighted in how last season played out. It was basically all you could have hoped for. Love matured as the season went on and became a solid QB. You found some good play from your receivers. Your RB’s were good, and now that spot has been potentially upgraded with Jacobs. Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is it really fair that NFL rookie contracts for draftees are set purely by one’s draft position with no cost of living adjustment whatsoever such that Brock Purdy almost won the Super Bowl for San Francisco yet was still stuck living with a roommate?
Answer: You want to play in this league? You abide by its rules, fair or unfair (this isn’t unfair). And Purdy is an anomaly of great magnitude. First, he’s actually far outperformed his contract - that’s not completely common. Second, he happens to live and play in one of the most expensive markets in the league. Third, no one was forcing him to live with anyone - that’s his choice. Even in San Francisco, you can get an apartment for $2500. He could live nicely for $5–$8k a month. If he paid $5k a month for an apartment that would be $60k a year, less than 10% of his annual salary. And Purdy is married now, so he’s not living with a teammate any longer. Cost of living adjustment? The contracts are only 3–4 years. Purdy will be getting an incredibly hefty raise before the 2025 season. Cost of living goes up about 3.5% a year. Purdy made $724k as a rookie. He’s up to $1 million this year. I don’t math very well, but I’d say his increases are over 3.5%.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How do NFL defenses handle pick plays when in man coverage?
Answer: Poorly, usually. Picks are illegal plays, where an offensive player intentionally runs into or blocks a defensive player from covering a person out to receive a pass. The best case scenario is to hope the official sees the pick occurring and throws a flag on the offense. Worst is the pick is missed and you get picked out of the play. Somewhere in between is the official sees a “rub” which is similar to a pick but not egregious. The pick is a blatant block; the rub is where people run through the same area and you may get lost in the wash. You may have defenders switch on potential picks. Maybe a corner is about to get picked but he and the slot corner have predetermined that the corner will always take the outside guy, regardless of whom that is. It’s a tough ask because it could require a change of direction for one or both of them.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What percentage chance do you give Dak Prescott of eventually signing a new contract with the Dallas Cowboys?
Answer: Less than 50/50. I think if the deal was going to get done, it would have gotten done already. Dallas isn’t winning the big games. And Dak hasn’t been at his best when the stakes are highest. So, while he’s a solid QB for regular games, he’s not solid against the best in the league, nor in the playoffs. They have to decide whether they want to simply continue to be OK, or if they want to try and become the early 90’s Cowboys again. Dak probably can’t get you there. I don’t know who can, but it doesn’t seem that Dak can give you more than he has thus far. I think they move on. Unless they buck the trend and win the SB this year - and we know that’s not happening - there’s not a good reason to overpay that particular guy.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why did Dakorien Moore decommit from LSU?
Answer: LSU has some VERY deep pockets to help recruit kids to the school. But they don’t have the depth of pocket of Texas. Or Phil Knight at Oregon, which is Moore’s second choice. I think LSU did a great job recruiting. And they had Moore, the #1 receiver prospect in the country, as well as the #1/2 RB prospect (Harlem Berry)in the country, AND the #1 QB recruit in the country (Bryce Underwood). I think Moore was really interested in being part of that. I think all the #1’s got together and recruited each other, choosing the play together to begin a strong 3–4 year run at LSU. But I think his heart was always at Texas. He’s from Texas, he has family in Austin. It’s less than 200 miles from Duncanville High to Austin, less than 3 hours on the road. Maybe it’s the money - Texas certainly has a bunch of money to work with in recruiting and NIL deals. But I think being closer to home on a team that believes it will be a top 10 contender factored in too.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why do teams with worse statistics often win in sports?
Answer: If we’re talking about professional sports, it’s because every team has professional athletes on it. They are the best of the best. Often the difference between winning and losing is a much smaller difference than people realize. Bad stats could be because of many things; and bad stats aren’t always completely indicative of a bad team. Could be a major injury to a key player, could be bad breaks. That said, typically teams with worse statiistics don’t win very often. More times than not the numbers indicate some basic flaws that need to be addressed.

Question: Do you think CeeDee Lamb's contract situation will be a distraction for the Cowboys this season?

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What does a one-and-a-half gap defensive front look like?
Answer: Here is a good look at a gap and a half front. The nose tackle is playing a zero technique, head up on the center. He’s responsible for either A gap. The defensive ends in this play (3–4 defense) are playing a 4i technique - they are lined up on the inside shoulder of the offensive tackles. They have responsibility for their B gaps, but they are squeezing down towards the center, so they are basically also giving aid to the A gap, creating a gap and a half - their B gap, plus assisting the A gap. The OLBs do a similar job, playing the C gap, but spying the B gap as well. This is a great run stuffing defensive call - you take away the A and B gaps and force the runner to bounce outside, where you have a LB or safety waiting.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do Americans tend to despise rugby, seeing it as a old version of American football?
Answer: I won’t speak for all Americans, but I’ll speak for myself - I don’t really know rugby enough to dislike it. What I’ve seen, I’ve enjoyed, but I’m a sports junkie. I’d venture a guess that most Americans are similar in the sense that rugby is such a fringe sport here, that it doesn’t get enough attention to be disliked. Though there are professional leagues here, it doesn’t have a major media contract, so it’s not in front of a lot of people regularly. We have a professional team here in New Orleans, and while their marketing team does a very good job of getting the word out, it’s still not enough to draw big crowds or get a lot of attention in the local media. So no, I - maybe we - don’t despise it. We just don’t follow it enough.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do professional golfers use the same driver for every hole?
Answer: Typically, golfers only carry a singular one wood (or one metal, as is more the case today), also known as a driver. There have been occasions where golfers carried two drivers, but those are rare. You are only allowed to carry 14 clubs in a stipulated round, so you have to think carefully about what clubs you put in your bag. As well, driver isn’t hit on every hole. On the PGA Tour, every golfer is great and they can all hit the ball a very long way with all of their clubs. So there may be holes on which they don’t need to hit the driver. Driver is almost never used on a par 3 hole. Those holes rarely measure over 250 yards long, which for a PGA tour player is usually a long iron or maybe a hybrid club type of shot. On the holes on which they hit the driver, typically - yes - it is the same driver for all of those holes. But some holes require more precision over power, so they may go for a three-wood, hybrid, or long iron off the tee instead of a driver.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: This NFL schedule sure is crazy. Why does the league keep sending teams like Miami, San Francisco, and New Orleans to "deep freeze" places like Green Bay, Cleveland, and Buffalo in December?
Answer: The schedule is the schedule. Today, we already know all but 3 teams every NFL team will play every year to infinity, or until the schedule changes (coming soon, the 18 game schedule). We know WHO those teams are because of the scheduling formula. What we don’t know is when they’ll go there, what time of the season. Some are just going to happen - Miami is in the same division as Buffalo, so they’ll play twice a year, once in Miami and once in Buffalo. For Miami, all they can do is hope the schedule makers put their Buffalo trip before November. As a Saints fan, I can’t complain much - we went to Cleveland in below zero wind chills in December of 2022. Actual game time temp was 9 degrees. But we’ve been lucky enough have been spared a lot of cold games, really. We went to Green Bay last year, but in September, and we went to New England in October. After that Cleveland game, the following week we went to Philadelphia, but it was 54 degrees. Every season, many schedules will feature at least one team from a warmer clime playing a cold weather team at home. It’s just the way it shakes out. Every year can’t see teams only face the NFC South and AFC South.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What is the most admirable thing about Tiger Woods?
Answer: Admirable isn’t a quality reflected by his play necessarily. I do admire his game, but I don’t know if the game and the person are so intertwined that I’d say I admire that about him. Here’s what I do admire: Tenacity - he keeps fighting even though his body isn’t always up to the challenge Understanding - he knows that when he shows up, people come out to see him. He gets that he moves the needle and so he gives some so the game is better for his being there. Graciousness - not to mere mortals, I don’t know how kind he is to everyday people. But he’s been VERY gracious to young up and comers on Tour. When Tiger was setting out into the world, he had a lot of connection to guys like Nicklaus and Palmer and Player and Trevino. Those guys gave him a ton of advice and life lessons for the course as well as golf lessons. From many a tour professional, we’ve heard stories of Tiger inviting them over, or going to visit them. Or things as simple as a note or a text. Remember, these guys today are the guys who were very young children in the early 2000’s when Tiger was at the peak of his power. So Tiger is to them who Jack is to Tiger. It’s important for him to help foster the next generation of stars, and it’s good that he recognizes that and has become that person to them.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Are you surprised by Tiger Woods missing the cut at the PGA Championship?
Answer: Surprised? Not at all. It would have been more surprising for him to make the cut, honestly. Disappointed? Yeah, a bit. I was hoping not to see him contend, but to see him remain relevant in the conversation. He’s always going to be relevant, but unfortunately it’s now more for the wrong reasons. It’s because he’s not who he was. It’s hard to see the sun set on the careers of the all-time greats. Tiger’s sun is falling precipitously. He simply can’t command the ball around like he wants to, like he used to. And he doesn’t make every putt like he used to. He can’t practice or play as much as he did when he was GOAT hunting, so he’s not capable of doing all the things. He’s still a world class golfer, and make no mistake, without the back and neck injuries, the ugly divorce, or the car accident, time would still have taken something from him. But it’s so hard to not imagine what the golf world would look like had he not had the health issues.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What is the rule for a ball flying out of bounds in golf?
Answer: A golf ball hit to any area that is deemed out of bounds - that is beyond either a white line marking out of bounds, or beyond white stakes that designate out of bounds - is out of play. It may not be played from beyond the out of bounds markers, and the penalty for hitting the ball out of bounds is one stroke, plus the distance of that stroke. That means you will drop a ball as near as possible as where you took your last stroke and play another stroke from that spot, with a one stroke penalty. If you hit the ball OB from the tee, you may re-tee the ball and hit again, with a one stroke penalty. So ball hit OB is one stroke, you take a penalty stroke (stroke 2) and lose the distance, and then you tee up again and the next stroke you take from the tee will be your third stroke. Same goes from anywhere else on the course - if you hit from the fairway and the ball goes out of bounds, you MUST return to where you hit the previous shot, drop a ball as near as possible to where you just hit, and play your next shot from there, after a one stroke penalty. Few notes: If you hit the ball and you know or are questionable as to whether it has gone out of bounds, you should play a provisional ball. To do this, you announce to your playing partners or fellow competitors that you think your ball has gone OB and that you are hitting a provisional. You MUST announce that it is a provisional ball - if you do not, the ball that you drop and hit will become your ball in play, with penalty added. You will have been said to have abandoned the ball you previously hit. So you MUST announce the provisional. This helps to save time - if your ball went OB, now, you’ve (hopefully) got another ball in play and you’ll go by the rules of stroke and distance. If your original shot is not out of bounds, you MUST abandon the provisional and play the original ball as it lies. For pace of play concerns, some clubs have adopted the USGA Local Rule allowing for adaptation of the rules. Instead of a stroke and distance penalty, you may not take the distance penalty - you may take a 2 stroke penalty, and you’d go and drop not more than 2 clublengths from the edge of the rough, in the fairway nearest where the ball went OB, no closer to the hole than where the ball went out. So you’d hit OB, then drop according to the local rule with a two stroke penalty, and play your 4th shot from that spot.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why has American football never spread significantly in Europe? Why do Europeans prefer soccer?
Answer: Probably a lot of reasons. First, the rules of soccer were codified in England, so while it’s origins may not be in England, the rules were decided in England. So just as American football is a very American sport, soccer is a very British sport. And exporting from England to Europe is much easier than from America. Also, Europe still plays a lot of rugby. That is their preferred alternative to soccer. As well, the rules and equipment for football all are very involved. With helmets and shoulder pads and all the other gear, it’s expensive. Soccer, you need a ball and some piece of surface area. Typically a field, but could be anything. Yeah, a goal is nice, but two t-shirts on the ground can define a goal area. And the rules are endless for football, as well as the strategy. There is strategy for soccer to be certain, but they aren’t as complex, and the rules are very simple. But the biggest reason may be the simplest one. Americans - as they are wont to do - didn’t really bother explaining the game or grassroots growing the game in Europe. They simply said “we love our game, you should love it too - here it is”, and went after it. The best way to grow the game is to actually teach it from the ground up. Explain how it works, what it is, and show people the game behind the game. Export flag football, which is only slightly more expensive than soccer. In this way, you learn the nuances and rudimentary rules of the game, as opposed to trying to digest everything at once. In short, we failed to give them the game they way we learned the game - we shoved it down their throats. And they didn’t really like it like that. Soccer will always be more popular. It’s the world’s game. Everyone can play, and it’s cheap. That will always be the difference maker - it’s not expensive, requires little, and it’s easy to learn to play.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How does signing an incorrect scorecard lead to disqualification in golf tournaments?
Answer: Each day during a tournament when a round ends, you are to turn in your scorecard, signed by you - which is your affidavit saying that these numbers are true and accurate. That is still today, the only way a score is accepted. Despite all the technologies that exist, the bottom line is the score you turn in to the official scorer is your official score. So obviously, when you sign on a card that has a score you didn’t shoot, trouble could ensue. Now if you shot a 72 and sign and return a card that says 73 or more, you are not disqualified because you’ve penalized yourself a stroke or more. It’s only when you turn in a scorecard for a number lower than what you shot that there is an issue. When you return a scorecard for a number lower than your actual score, it’s as though you are cheating the system and the field. Even if you’re not intentionally trying to cheat, it projects as such, and in reality it is an aggression to the field. To protect the field, you have to disqualify that person. In golf, it’s one of the more egregious errors there is.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What is the ruling in golf when a shot goes off course but then comes back onto the course? Is this considered a legal or illegal shot?
Answer: It’s a legal shot. Where the ball comes to rest is the major part of the ruling. It a ball were to hit a tree out of bounds but return to the course, then that ball is in play. It’s about where it lies when it is no longer n motion.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is it against the rules to leave a golf ball in the hole?
Answer: Not at all. Once holed, you are under no oblilgation beyond etiquette to remove your ball from the hole. When playing with pace, sometimes, people leave their ball in the hole just to keep things moving. Not on the PGA Tour necessarily, but in regular rounds.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: In the NFL, when an O-Lineman reports eligible on 1st down, can another player who was also already on the field switch to the eligible man (by reporting to the ref) on 2nd down?
Answer: Yes. Every individual down is a new play, so a different person can be eligible every play, but they must always report as eligible.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: How likely is it for the leader after 36 holes to win the PGA Championship?
Answer: According to stats, it’s about 50/50. About half of the 36 hole leaders of majors have gone on to win the tournament. That number is relatively the same for having the 54 hole lead. Recently that number has been challenged as only about 37% of 54-hole leaders have closed the deal.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: I saw a PGA match today where the player’s ball went waaaaay out of bounds into the concession area and landed against the wall behind a water fountain. How is he expected to play that?
Answer: Well, they’re not expected to play that. But how they proceed is the issue. If this was the PGA Championship, it could be that the area in which it landed isn’t permanent - that this was an concession area placed on the course for this particular event. IF that is the case, then the golfer would get relief from the obstruction and get to take a drop with no penalty. The assumption there is if this weren’t a golf tournament, the object would not be there, so you would not have to play from this place with these conditions - in that case, the relief is free. However, if the obstruction is permanent - maybe a restroom building or a physical building - then any relief taken would be with a one stroke penalty.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is the arrest of Scottie Scheffler outside Valhalla before Day 2 of the 2024 PGA Championship all much ado about nothing?
Answer: It is not much ado about nothing. A volunteer lost their life on that morning, so it cannot be seen as nothing. I feel horrible not only for the person, but also the bus driver that has to live with that for the rest of their life. This was a tragedy. As for Scheffler, we don’t know and really can’t know until this is done. But it sounds like something. I’ll say this - I do not believe he will be jailed. I do think he made an error. As we weren’t there, we can’t tell how the traffic was being routed, or how this was or wasn’t a violation of the orders of the police. If he seriously didn’t know in the confusion, that is understandable - often police will give one order for traffic and then counter that. Plus, Scottie was going to a place that no others were going. That said, if he disobeyed the cop (this would be a nice time to hear from all those “just comply” folks from a few years back…) and drove with the cop “attached” to the vehicle, then he’s got an issue. That can’t be “nothing”. I think they drop the aggravated assault on an officer charge so he won’t have a felony. They stick him with the misdemeanors, make him pay a hefty fine and maybe he has to do community service or attend a class. It may end up being played as less than it was. But it seems to be something.

Question: Is Saquon Barkley's return to MetLife Stadium in Week 7 against the New York Giants a must-watch game on the Philadelphia Eagles' schedule?

Question: Will the Chiefs add a receiver in 2024?

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why do NFL left tackles have higher average salaries than even quarterbacks do? Does that mean that left tackles are even more important than QB’s (on average)? Shouldn’t teams the focus their draft strategies upon selecting quality left tackles?
Answer: First, let’s fact check a bit. There are only 2 guys who are potential starting QBs in 2024 who are not still on their rookie deals, Minshew and Darnold who have “low” average salaries. For purposes of this discussion, we should not include rookies and players on their rookie deals because they cannot earn the same. Beyond that, every single starting QB except Geno Smith makes more money than any starting tackle. And Smith ($25m) is only behind Penei Sewell ($28m), who is the highest paid tackle in the game, for salary. So left tackles don’t have higher average salaries than starting QBs. So the rest of the statement doesn’t come to pass. LT’s are not more important than QB’s. But if you don’t have a solid starting LT, your QB’s blindside isn’t secure and you run the risk of losing that high paid QB. And teams do focus their draft strategies on selecting the best left tackles. Typically, the first offensive linemen off the board are left tackles. The first three linemen selected in this draft were left tackles. (Latham was drafted to play left tackle, though he played right tackle at Alabama). The first one selected last year was a left tackle. So it’s obvious that is always a position of concern for NFL teams.

Question: Are golfers good at mini-golf?
Answer: Maybe, but not necessarily. Even on an actual golf course, most golfers will admit that putting is it’s own game, away from the tee to green game. This is one place where with practice an average person with great touch, feel, and imagination, can play on a level relatively similar to a tour professional. There is skill to putting, but it’s a skill that common folks can learn more easily than learning to hit a 320 yard drive or hitting 200 yard 6-irons, or hitting approach shots consistently to 15 feet. But the thing about it is mini-golf isn’t always the same. Some mini-golf courses are fairly straight forward, where you simply line the putt up and hit. Others are more complex, where you must dodge obstacles or bounce off of walls - things that you’d never fine on a real golf course. So the concept of a smooth stroke might be similar, but the parameters don’t have much correlation beyond that.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Is it harder to golf in the rain?
Answer: 100%. Personally, I don’t play in the rain if I don’t have to… Rain makes everything different, from beginning to end. Wet grips are harder to hold onto. Water on the ball and the face of the club have a minor impact on the ball’s performance. Balls on the fairway will have water on them, which can have an effect on contact, ball flight will be lessened. Balls won’t roll out on the fairways. In the rough, wet grass is harder to get through than dry grass. Around the greens, you have to be careful of moisture affecting your shot. In bunkers, the sand gets firmer and packs tighter, so getting under and through becomes more challenging. On the green, the ball will not roll quite as far or efficiently, and line could be affected because balls will slow down more quickly. When it rains, you get wet too, and your clothes get wet, impeding your swing. You may put on a rain suit, but that also affects how you swing the club, which you’re already having an issue holding onto due to wet grips. It’s a slog…

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: In golf, if the wind blows the ball off the tee and it keeps rolling into the hole, will the hole count as 0 strokes?
Answer: Mr. Port’s answer is correct. A ball must be deliberately and intentionally struck with a stroke for it to be in play. If a ball comes off the tee due to falling, or a wind gust, or -even- a practice stroke, it MUST be replaced, with no penalty to the golfer. That MUST is important in golf rules - you’ll often see the terms should and must in the Rules of Golf. Should is a suggestion; Must is an absolute for which there is a penalty is assessed if you do not follow the rule. I’d love to see the course where a wind would blow a ball off the tee and have it roll into the hole. I’ve played some courses where the tee is elevated and maybe the hole is some distance downhill. Maybe that could happen? But SO very unlikely. Either way, the ball cannot be put in play without a stroke, so there is no such thing as a zero stroke hole.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Rather than judging team draft strategies solely by draft busts, shouldn’t NFL pundits judge teams by the totality of their drafting success? If a team pursues a high risk, high-reward strategy of drafting many busts but also many stars, is that bad?
Answer: Personally, I think drafts aren’t really able to be evaluated until at least 3 years into the future. By that time every player has had time to learn the game and become who they’re going to be. I know fantasy football isn’t the best way to evaluate, but there is a concept in fantasy football called the 3rd year receiver. The third year a receiver is in the league, if he’s going to be good, that is the year they typically take a large step forward. But that’s not an uncommon theme for many positions. The first year, you’re just trying to hang on. The second year, you become comfortable with what other people are doing. Third season, you’re comfortable in your own skin as well as knowing the playbook inside and out. That’s the best time to evaluate how a draft was. Sure it’s fun to MMQB. And sure, it’s nice to speculate based on what a player’s college performance/NFL projection is. But until you see the players in action with at least a full season under their belt, you have no idea. And let’s be honest - no team goes into a draft thinking “I’m taking high risk/high reward guys across the board”. That wouldn’t be a prudent strategy. If you draft thinking star or bust, you’re not fixing your team. Every team needs guys they can count on. You hope everyone you draft becomes the best at their position. But the reality is if you can get a team full of top 10 in the league players at their spot, you’re going to be successful, whether they’re the absolute best at their spot or not. Your first 2–3 rounds of the draft should be low risk guys because you’re counting on them to be contributors soon.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What happens if you go to college for four years playing football but don't get drafted into the National Football League (NFL)?
Answer: Likely, you’ll end up just like the rest of us… in the job market. Sure, you may be asked to tryout as an undrafted free agent. Or you may take it upon yourself to simply ask to be invited to a camp for OTA’s. But the reality is 0.41% of all college students in any given year make it to the NFL. There are over 81,000 people playing college football every year. In 2023, 259 players were drafted. In 2023, 672 players were invited to training camp as undrafted free agents or guys just invited to try out. Of all those players, 297 rookies made opening day rosters. So the stark reality is, you’re not likely going to the NFL even if you go to school for 4 years. The vast majority of players end up getting work-a-day jobs like us.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Do you believe that expanding the College Football Playoff to include at least 12 teams will enhance or diminish the excitement of the championship games?
Answer: If you mean the conference championship games, I think it will diminish them, but only in some places. For instance in the SEC, both teams will get into the playoffs, so the championship only means you get seeded higher in the playoffs. Ditto for the Big10. Where it gets interesting is for the other conferences. Yeah, the winners of all the Power5 conferences will get in. But maybe a loser in one of those conferences doesn’t make it. Maybe a 9–3 West Virginia type team goes to the Big12 Championship and loses and doesn’t get into the playoffs. So that may mean that the Big12 Championship has more meaning because Oklahoma State or whomever steps up to be the new big dog in that conference may need to win to ensure their place in the playoff. Because despite possibly becoming also-rans in the Big10 or the SEC, teams like Texas, Oklahoma, USC and UCLA will still get more credit. Those teams with 2-3 losses, even if they don’t make their conference championship, will be more likely to play in the playoffs than a West Virginia type team who may play in the conference championship. I’m already on record as not being the biggest fan of the 12-soon-to-be-16 team playoff. And I think in general, it will diminish conference championships as well as conference play. The more teams you let in, the less you have to do to get in. And if you mean the national championship game, that’s going to be the same because poorer college teams don’t stand much a chance against the very good college teams. As for the playoffs, Ms. Fowler has it down in her answer. You’re going to get one good matchup and the rest will be *meh*…. And when you get that matchup of teams facing each other for the 3rd time in a season (though that won’t happen because “magically”, teams will move up or down a spot so they don’t end up facing off, lest the committee create a matchup no one wants to see…), be prepared for footballmageddon.

Question: What were Rory McIlroy’s "personal and professional commitments" when he resigned from the PGA Tour Player Board?

When Monahan pulled the rug from under them, saying they were looking to get in bed with LIV and the PIF, Rory felt dumb, so he backed up a while, then completely left the Player Board. It was all those things combined, as well as the time and committment of trying to be everywhere all the time at every moment that took a toll on him and his game. So he left the board and began to work on himself and his game. And the results are in - beyond a less than stellar T33 at Hilton Head, he’s been strong in his last 5 starts. T22 at the Masters, a 3rd at the Valero, and back to back wins in his last 2 starts.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What does being tackled in American football feel like?
Answer: This is a question that can’t be easily answered because there is no “one size fits all” tackle. There are some tackles that are like when you’re a small kid and your large dog knocks you over. Pretty innocuous, no great shakes. There are some where you don’t get up. Most of them are in between those two, but understand that the range is vast. Most tackles hurt at least a little, whether it’s on the hit end or the hitting the turf end. But the adrenaline pumping through you from the game itself often numbs you to what’s really going on. You don’t really feel the pain. If you were a normal human and you were tackled like this, it would be a big deal. In a football game, you don’t feel it the same way. Plus a football player’s body is more conditioned to hits like this. They practice hitting, so they are more prepared for it. Plus, with the training done, your body is harder and can withstand the tackle better. Suffice it to say more times than not, it doesn’t feel good. But it doesn’t really hurt unless you fall awkwardly.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Recently, the NBA All-Star game has become boring. What format should the league come up with to bring excitement back to the event?
Answer: Do like football and quit playing the game. Baseball seems to be the only sport that can have an All-Star game and actually have the participants play hard. Basketball’s game is during the season. No one will play defense because it’s hard and no one wants to get hurt. The only solution I can think of is to have new rules, like street court rules. Make em, take em. Play games to 10. That way, you either D up to win and run the court, or you give up the court. Instead of some long drawn out affair, create three 5 man teams from each conference, and let them play half court games to 10. Or play three man teams, so everyone has to carry some weight. Or just have skills challenges and go home. But what is happening now is a waste. You’re doing the fans absolutely no favors with what they’ve been doing.
